title: Measuring and Attributing Evidence Sensitivity in Medical Vision-Language Models via Symmetric Counterfactual Controls
abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) asked closed clinical questions ("Is there a polyp?") can score well by relying on the question rather than the image, and current hallucination benchmarks cannot separate true visual discrimination from editing shortcuts or shifts in the answer threshold. We introduce a Counterfactual Evidence Framework that pairs each lesion erasure with a shape- and tool-matched control edit elsewhere in the image, adds same-site ring controls, restored and partial erasures, degraded views and natural negatives, tests on held-out inpainting tools, separates discrimination (the Evidence Sensitivity Gap, ESG, and AUROC) from the answer threshold, and checks the labels with blinded physician readers and hidden-state probes. Across 507 main-test cases (1,115 views), nine frontier VLMs claim 41.1% to 61.6% of erased lesions (ESG 0.269 to 0.470), whereas MedScope-4B, a Qwen3.5-4B agent trained on automatically built counterfactual trajectories, claims 9.6% (ESG 0.758; p <= 0.001 in all 27 primary comparisons). Physician readers support automated erasure in colonoscopy, where frontier models still claim 45% of erased lesions against 1% for MedScope-4B, but call a finding present on 54.7% of pooled erased reads across all sources, which bounds what unverified erasure can certify. Across 12 pre-registered training or system arms and 270 decision policies screened under a rule fixed in advance, every apparent utility gain comes from shifting the threshold rather than improving held-out discrimination, and probes point to perception as the remaining limit. We also report a 0/48 pneumothorax failure on an external cohort; retraining with pneumothorax patients in every stage finds 53% of pneumothoraxes on new patients without changing the main-test results.

title: A Latching Recovery Funnel for Neural Swing-Up Controllers of N -Link Cart–Pendulums
abstract: Abstract Neural swing-up controllers for multi-link cart–pendulum systems are typically optimized from a canonical initial condition in which the pendulum chain hangs at rest. We demonstrate that, although such controllers can successfully swing up and stabilize systems comprising (N=1)–(4) links from rest, their ability to recover from large disturbances is severely limited. Across 200 randomly generated knock-down states for each link configuration, the controller achieves a recovery rate of 97% for (N=1), but no more than 1% for (N\geq2). This degradation arises because the memoryless swing-up policy continues to inject control forces when the system enters states that lie substantially outside the trajectories encountered during training. To address this limitation, we introduce a recovery-funnel architecture integrated into the original feed-forward neural network through a compact, analytically designed control circuit. The proposed architecture comprises three functional components: (i) a downward-position linear quadratic regulator (LQR) damper that drives the cart towards its central equilibrium while bringing the pendulum links to rest; (ii) a detector neuron that identifies the downward-rest configuration; and (iii) a single self-recurrent rectified linear unit (ReLU) latch neuron that maintains activation of the swing-up control branch for a prescribed duration. The resulting architecture employs only ReLU and sinusoidal activation units, respects the original parameter bounds by keeping all weights below the prescribed limit, and preserves the nominal control behaviour. Simulation results demonstrate a substantial improvement in disturbance recovery, achieving successful recovery in all 200/200 trials for every configuration with (N\in{1,2,3,4}). Furthermore, the controller successfully recovers from all 24 extreme disturbance scenarios involving strong external pushes and impulsive tip-yank perturbations. These improvements come at the expense of increased recovery time, with median values ranging from 3.3 s for the single-link system to 12.6 s for the four-link configuration. The proposed recovery funnel relies on exact convergence to the downward-rest state in a noise-free simulation environment, which introduces important limitations regarding robustness to measurement noise, modelling uncertainties, and real-world implementation. These limitations are discussed alongside the implications of the proposed architecture. The source code, trained models, and evaluation framework are made openly available to facilitate reproducibility and further investigation.

title: Attention at Absolute Zero
abstract: Attention scores candidate supports of an answer, which we call witnesses, and reads the scores at a temperature. We build a higher-order attention layer whose state lives on pairs of items: for a pair (a, b), each third item k is a witness judged through its legs (a, k) and (k, b). It reads witnesses at zero temperature, keeping the best and the number tied with it, passes on only bits comparing such counts, rebuilds its pair state from the input and these bits at every loop, and is trained from answers alone. Each choice removes one way soft attention fails at size: dispersed weight, unresolved gaps between learned scores, and a drifting soft state. In maximum retrieval it is right on at least 99.95% of sets 1,000 times larger than in training, on all ten seeds; trained with a soft count, the same network falls to 42% at 4,096 items. On CLRS-30 without hints, a general form of the layer (half its channels read at zero temperature, numbers embedded, state carried) beats the best published model, which uses hints on some tasks; the full cold layer is exact on every test input of 9 of the 12 tasks whose answers depend on numbers only through comparisons. From yes-or-no answers it decides 2-SAT and two-colouring exactly at 500 variables and, as our theory predicts, not parity equations. Beside a frozen 7B language model it chains family relations exactly at 1,000 statements after training on 16, where the model alone falls to 44%; finite checks on the weights prove every block that learned correct at every size, on acyclic contexts and given what the model reads. On CLUTRR it is right on every story of five to ten relations given the graphs, learning the 62 rules exactly; from text, with the model frozen, no hand-written rule and only a small read-in trained, it lifts an open 7B model from 33% to 65%, above every system we found without hand-written rules except frontier reasoning models.

title: Event-Based Dynamic Lip Region Estimation During Speech
abstract: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and low power consumption, making them promising for speech-related applications. These include automatic lip reading, audiovisual speech analysis, and human-robot interaction, particularly in challenging environments characterized by low illumination or high dynamic range. Event-based lip reading, speaker recognition, and voice activity detection, however, mostly operate on a cropped region of interest (ROI), by hand or by the dataset, and no event-based method supplies that ROI as a spatial region; existing event-based face analysis gives the mouth as landmarks, which presents a mismatch between application and localization. The present work predicts a dense heatmap over the lip region from the full event "frame". Events are encoded as a polarity-separated voxel grid and processed at every location by a two-pathway continuous-time recurrent network (CT-RNN) with learned, log-space bounded time constants acting on the real elapsed time of each bin: a stateless fast pathway and a stateful slow pathway, utilised for refining and anchoring the prediction. The model reaches 69.5% on lips on four unseen speakers and switches target only 2.1 times per second, against 8.9 and 11.0 for convolutional baselines with more parameters. Adding a spatial encoder improves precision but fails on a new face scale. On a real event sensor, trained only on simulated events, the proposed model reaches 58.0% on lips against 43.2% for the CNN, with fewer than half its target switches.

title: Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows. This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. Rather than focusing on language understanding alone, NLPg conceptualises prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts that externalise goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and intermediate reasoning states. Prompting is thus not merely a technical interaction technique, but a form of dialogic cognitive programming operating within distributed human/AI memory architectures. Building on theories of distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning, the paper proposes the notion of Dialogic Working Memory, describing how prompts and conversational states function as temporary external memory structures supporting reasoning continuity and reflective regulation. We further map existing memory architectures (BTMA, SKGE, RMR) onto this framework, illustrating how episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers support long-horizon conversational coherence. Finally, implications for computational linguistics and AI/mediated knowledge systems are discussed, suggesting a post symbolic and post interface paradigm in which natural language operates simultaneously as communication medium, executable specification, cognitive scaffold, and distributed memory architecture.

title: Hidden-State Similarity Predicts Re-Elicitation After Inoculation Prompting
abstract: Fine-tuning on narrow harmful tasks can cause emergent misalignment, where models generalize harmful behavior beyond the training distribution. Inoculation prompting can reduce this effect by explicitly eliciting the undesired behavior during training, but recent work shows that the behavior can reappear when evaluation prompts contain cues from the training context. We study what makes such prompts effective triggers. We find that, surprisingly, textual similarity to the inoculation prompt is an incomplete predictor. Instead, prompts are more likely to re-elicit suppressed behavior when they induce activation states similar to those produced by the inoculation context. These findings advance our understanding of how inoculation prompting modulates conditional misalignment, and suggest that activation space analysis can help identify when suppressed behaviors remain accessible under eval-time prompts.

title: Can GenAI numeracy tutors support self-regulated learning?
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been the focus of much attention in the higher education sector, both for its potential to support personalised and adaptive learning, but also due to the risk that students may outsource learning to it, leading to gaps in their professional or discipline competencies. This risk of cognitive offloading applies equally to learning how to learn, a skill set explored through studies of self-regulated learning (SRL). Two GenAI numeracy tutors were piloted at a regional Australian university as one component of a newly launched mathematics and statistics support centre, one focusing on medication calculations for Nursing students (NiNA), and the other on threshold numeracy skills for Education students (EdNA). Detailed analysis of students’ conversations with these agents using Zimmerman and Moylan’s 2009 SRL framework revealed extensive evidence of some elements of SRL such as strategic planning, task-specific strategies, and adaptive competence; trace evidence of other elements including self-efficacy and self-evaluation; and no evidence of the remaining elements. This study contributes an underrepresented qualitative perspective to the body of research into the crossover of GenAI and SRL and foreshadows avenues for further research and refinements in the design of GenAI numeracy tutors.

title: What's in a Tree ? Hierarchical $n$-gram models as controlled approximators of language
abstract: Hierarchical models have been proposed as synthetic settings for studying language. However, their relevance to realistic language corpora remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce tree-grams, autoregressive generative $n$-gram models that build the conditional probability tensor $p(x_n \mid x_{1:n-1})$ through a hierarchical composition of order-2 and order-3 tensors. $n$ controls the maximal context window, whereas a rank hyperparameter $d$ controls model capacity, yielding an interpretable and systematically scalable family of approximators of language. We show how tree-grams outperform existing $n$-gram baselines, while remaining competitive with deep transformer-based language models. We demonstrate the utility of such controlled approximations by using tree-grams as generative models. In particular, we show that hyperparameter transfer under $μ$P can be made more robust when narrower models are tuned on simpler data, generated by tree-grams with moderate $n$ and $d$. In addition, we show that entropy and effective range of correlations control performance gap after fine-tuning. This is because tree-grams allow us to explicitly control horizon and capacity. When allowed to route across candidate topologies, we observe emergent sparsity in tree-grams. Such concentrated routing permits pruning upto 95\% of topologies without significant change in performance.

evidence.title: What's in a Tree ? Hierarchical $n$-gram models as controlled approximators of language
evidence.abstract: Hierarchical models have been proposed as synthetic settings for studying language. However, their relevance to realistic language corpora remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce tree-grams, autoregressive generative $n$-gram models that build the conditional probability tensor $p(x_n \mid x_{1:n-1})$ through a hierarchical composition of order-2 and order-3 tensors. $n$ controls the maximal context window, whereas a rank hyperparameter $d$ controls model capacity, yielding an interpretable and systematically scalable family of approximators of language. We show how tree-grams outperform existing $n$-gram baselines, while remaining competitive with deep transformer-based language models. We demonstrate the utility of such controlled approximations by using tree-grams as generative models. In particular, we show that hyperparameter transfer under $μ$P can be made more robust when narrower models are tuned on simpler data, generated by tree-grams with moderate $n$ and $d$. In addition, we show that entropy and effective range of correlations control performance gap after fine-tuning. This is because tree-grams allow us to explicitly control horizon and capacity. When allowed to route across candidate topologies, we observe emergent sparsity in tree-grams. Such concentrated routing permits pruning upto 95\% of topologies without significant change in performance.

title: BugGen 2.0: Rethinking the Roles of LLMs for Scalable RTL Bug Synthesis
abstract: AI-assisted RTL localization and debugging need ground-truth bug datasets with known locations and observable failures, while testbench grading uses injected bugs to measure detection capability. Creating such datasets at scale remains a major EDA challenge. BugGen 1.0 shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate context-aware RTL mutations. Still, it relies on the model for both choosing where to mutate and generating the edit, which increases inference costs and can lead to invalid choices. BugGen 2.0 changes this division of labor. Deterministic algorithms handle structural analysis, target selection, and validation, while the LLM focuses on localized semantic rewriting. Across four OpenTitan IP blocks and FabScalar with three LLMs, BugGen 2.0 reaches every requested quota of compilable bug scenarios that cause at least two test failures, with 14-16 of 16 configured mutation types represented. In completed same-model comparisons, it reduces token use by 6.8x-15.4x relative to BugGen 1.0 and 1.5x-7.9x relative to Firefly. BugGen 2.0 also expands the dataset without simulating every new bug. After finding accepted scenarios with observable failures, it generates alternative mutations at the same locations, simulates only a subset, and estimates acceptance for the rest. This skips 63.6% of AES and 33.9% of FabScalar variant simulations. Full simulation finds that 77.7% of AES variants and 95.2% of FabScalar variants are accepted, with a 1.09% estimation error on the directly comparable FabScalar set. These results show that focusing LLMs on semantic rewriting lowers inference and simulation cost while improving consistency across models and designs.

title: Bridging the articulation gap: A multi-agent conversational AI platform for compassionate scaffolding of technical interview skills
abstract: Technical job interviews place computing students under pressure to demonstrate algorithmic and communication skills simultaneously under live observation, producing what we term the articulation gap. Existing preparation pathways provide only partial support: coding platforms ignore communication, coaching is economically inaccessible, and current AI simulators remain reactive. We present AIView, a multi-agent conversational platform that scaffolds integrated interview competencies. A LangGraph orchestrator coordinates specialised agents for question delivery and adaptive guidance alongside verbalisation monitors and an affect-aware tone layer, with assessments anchored in the SOLO taxonomy. An evaluation with 31 students showed high usability (SUS = 73.8), strong trust in AI feedback (M = 3.94), and high recommendation intent (M = 4.29). Participants valued personalised, code-aware feedback and a low-pressure learning environment. By fostering compassionate human-AI collaboration that supports creative problem solving and connection in a digital learning environment, AIView represents a step towards democratising access to career preparation through adaptive scaffolding.

title: Event-Based Person Detection for Maritime UAV Search
abstract: Maritime search and rescue requires locating people in the water quickly, motivating the use of UAVs to survey the search area. During flight, camera motion and the longer exposures used in low light can blur small targets and hinder person detection. Event cameras record brightness changes as they occur, reducing the motion blur associated with longer exposure times. We investigate their use for maritime person detection by generating synthetic events using the v2e event simulator from public MOBDrone rescue videos and retaining the existing annotations. We compare the recurrent vision transformer model RVT-T with YOLOv8n and RT-DETR-R18 trained on exposure-matched images. On 843 test samples from held-out recordings, RVT-T achieves 15.63% person AP50:95, compared with 6.89% for YOLOv8n and 9.44% for RT-DETR-R18 under 100 ms synthetic exposure. Increasing exposure times from 50 to 200 ms progressively reduces frame-based detection accuracy, widening the gap to the event model. To evaluate the feasibility of on-board processing, we deploy our detector on a Jetson Orin Nano platform. The RVT-T model retains its accuracy and requires approximately 136 ms and 2.02 J per sample, allowing real-time processing on the UAV.

title: Transfer Once, Ask Locally: Compact Audio-Visual Memory for On-Device Question Answering
abstract: Audio-visual question answering on lightweight user devices requires balancing speed, memory usage, privacy, and communication. One approach is to run audio-visual encoders on a server and a lightweight language decoder on the user device, keeping questions local while offloading media encoding. However, transferring and processing the full multimodal representation remains costly. We propose a training-free, query-agnostic token pruning framework that constructs a compact, reusable memory before transmission. We define video spatio-temporal blocks and aligned audio windows as players and estimate their importance through Monte Carlo Shapley valuation. We use an embedding coverage objective that combines query-independent utility with cross-modal redundancy calibration and rewards unimodal diversity through marginal coverage gains. We retain the original token embeddings of high-scoring players under a limited token budget and transfer the resulting memory once for reuse across subsequent local questions. Experiments on Video-MME, Daily-Omni, and Video-Holmes using video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) and video-SALMONN 2 Pro (4B) show that our method achieves the best or tied-best QA accuracy among the compared compression methods across all evaluated settings. On Daily-Omni with video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) at 80\% pruning, our method improves accuracy by 12.86--14.62 percentage points over these methods while achieving the lowest device-side LLM prefill and decoding latency, with up to $1.92\times$ decoding speedup at comparable embedding memory usage.

title: Learning to Undo: Transfer Reinforcement Learning under State Space Transformations
abstract: Transfer learning in reinforcement learning (RL) has shown strong empirical success. In this work, we take a more principled perspective by studying when and how transferring knowledge between MDPs (a source and a target) can be provably beneficial. Specifically, we consider the case where there exists an undo map such that applying this map to the target's state space recovers the source exactly. We propose an algorithm that learns this map by matching state feature statistics gathered from both MDPs, and then uses it to transfer the source policy to the target. We theoretically justify the algorithm by analyzing the setting when the undo map is linear and the source is linearly-$Q^\star$ realizable, where our approach has strictly better sample complexity than tabula rasa RL in the target MDP. Empirically, we demonstrate that these benefits extend beyond this regime: on challenging continuous control tasks and Atari games, our method achieves significantly better sample efficiency. Overall, our results highlight how shared structure between tasks can be leveraged for efficient transfer of policies across environments.

title: Recipient-Focused Hallucinations in AI-Generated Professor Outreach Emails: A Pilot Factorial Evaluation of Grounding and Verification
abstract: Abstract Background : LLMs increasingly draft personalized academic outreach, which depends on describing a real professor's research. Unsupported claims about a recipient's topics, methods, or findings misrepresent their scholarly work. Methods : In an offline pilot, a 2 × 2 design varied whether the writer received a publication evidence packet during drafting and whether a verifier revised the draft afterwards (conditions A–D). We generated 96 emails for 12 professors across three fields, decomposed them into 360 atomic research claims, and labelled each against the professor's evidence packet with an automatic (LLM) evaluator. All primary estimates are pilot estimates from automatic labels, not human-verified measurements. Reliability was assessed against a blinded 36-claim human-labeled subset (10% of claims) and a second automatic evaluator from a third model family. Results : Under the primary evaluator, the closed-book baseline (A) had a Severe Error Rate (SER) of 0.344 (21/61 claims; exact 95% CI 0.227–0.477). Grounding the writer (B) produced no severe errors in 90 judged claims (0.000, CI 0.000–0.040) and raised Supported Personalization Density (SPD) from 0.65 to 1.71 supported claims per 100 words. Verify-only (C) left 1 severe error in 50 claims (0.020; SPD 1.04); grounded-plus-verified (D) produced none (0/87) at the highest specificity (1.76). Interpretation and limits: Primary-evaluator agreement with the human annotator was only fair (Cohen’s κ = 0.33, CI 0.16–0.49). The evaluator was too lenient in 14 of 16 disagreements, suggesting that the automatic severe-error rates may underestimate error prevalence. However, the small human-labelled subset does not establish the magnitude or direction of bias across the complete dataset. The zeros are evaluator-specific: a second evaluator relabelling the same claims found 10 severe errors in B and 4 in D, closed-book 0.455 - a large reduction under grounding, not elimination. And 17 of the 21 closed-book severe errors came from the four psychology professors; excluding that field, closed-book SER falls to 0.095. Both automatic evaluators reported lower pooled severe-error rates for grounded conditions than for ungrounded conditions. Grounding during drafting also showed a lower observed pooled SER than post-generation verification alone. Conclusion : Verified publication evidence sharply reduced severe misrepresentation - to zero under the primary evaluator, roughly four-fold under the second - while making emails more specific, and outperformed correcting drafts afterwards. Grounding, not correction alone, is the more promising safeguard; establishing the effect size needs human labelling at scale and a validated judge.

title: Colombo: A Frontier-to-Frontier Autoresearch System for Oracle-Based Optimization
abstract: Science advances from frontier to frontier as discoveries reshape what is known and create the basis for further discovery. We present Colombo, a self-organizing AI researcher that drives this renewal, first instantiated in oracle-based optimization. Here, the central question is how efficiently a problem class can be solved through a prescribed information interface and what costs no admissible algorithm can avoid. The gap between achievable guarantees and unavoidable limits defines the frontier recorded in its Complexity Atlas, a living map of frontier settings and the current state of knowledge. Self-Organization turns unresolved gaps into adaptive research programmes, coordinating conjecture formation, mathematical investigation, and replanning as evidence accumulates. Adversarial Co-Ascent develops algorithms and hard families through reciprocal challenge, exposing mechanisms of information use and concealment that guide stronger methods and proofs of unavoidable costs. Independent review and Lean-based formal certification check mathematical claims, while the Long-Term Memory carries supported findings and research experience across settings. To date, Colombo has established optimal or near-optimal rates for more than fifty settings in the Atlas. Colombo thus takes a concrete step toward Autopoietic Science: a scientific process whose validated advances regenerate the conditions of its own progress, continually reshaping how inquiry is organized and what it can discover.

title: UnrealEvent: Synthetic Dataset Generation and Annotation for Event-Based Vision
abstract: Event-based cameras provide high temporal resolution, low power consumption, and a high dynamic range, but progress in event-based object detection remains constrained by the scarcity of annotated training data. To solve this issue, this paper introduces the tool UnrealEvent, a synthetic dataset-generation pipeline implemented in Unreal Engine 5.5. The pipeline combines a V2E-inspired event-frame generator with EasySynth semantic-rendering passes, allowing rendered level sequences to be converted into paired event representations and YOLO-format bounding-box annotations without manual labeling. Events are generated from per-pixel log-luminance differences between consecutive frames, with contrast thresholds sampled independently from a normal distribution to emulate the fabrication-induced threshold mismatch of real sensors. Using this pipeline, we provide a synthetic dataset and evaluate YOLOv8 detectors under synthetic, zero-shot real, and real fine-tuning training on eTraM. The results show strong in-domain synthetic performance but a substantial synthetic-to-real gap, especially for pedestrians. Fine-tuning on a small real subset improves real-domain performance, while the remaining gap highlights the importance of asset diversity and sensor calibration.

title: Pareto-Informed Smart "Predict, then Optimize" for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Problems
abstract: Many real-world planning applications, from logistics, routing to resource allocation, give rise to optimization problems that need to balance multiple, conflicting objectives. While machine learning is often used to predict the unknown parameters or costs of these problems, standard models trained on prediction accuracy can lead to suboptimal plans. Decision-Focused Learning (DFL) addresses this by integrating the downstream optimization task into the training objective. However, existing DFL methods for multi-objective problems rely on simple scalarization, which fails to capture the rich trade-offs of the Pareto Frontier. To address this gap, we propose a Pareto-aware extension to single-objective Smart "Predict, then Optimize" (SPO+) for multi-objective combinatorial optimization problems. Our loss function leverages the true Pareto Frontier, forming a target decision that aligns with a sampled preference vector, and minimizes regret against this target. Experiments on multi-objective shortest path and multi-objective knapsack problems show that our approach outperforms traditional two-stage Mean Squared Error (MSE) baselines. It also surpasses scalarization-based SPO+ approaches.

title: SISE-N G1.330: Reproducible Data and Code for Distributed Endogenous Satisficing under Irreversible Mortality
abstract: This reproducibility archive accompanies a research manuscript on distributed endogenous satisficing in a two-dimensional survival environment. The primary experiment (SISE-N G1.330) evaluates four action-selection mechanisms in a matched 2 × 2 design: central bounded candidate acceptance with fixed or adaptive satisfaction thresholds, and direct distributed recurrent motor competition with fixed or adaptive local channel gains. Twelve seeded 15 × 15 maps were each evaluated under all four arms using an identical frozen population-Q checkpoint; each life was observed for at most 5,000 steps with irreversible simulated death. The archive contains 48 life summaries, 143,847 original executed physical steps, corresponding full decision logs, provenance and independent audit files, an executable source and checkpoint chain, 12 auditor-only map reconstructions, code-linked architecture documentation, original figures, and an English manuscript and supplement. Earlier G1.328–G1.329 auxiliary records (181,576 executed steps) are included for resource-context analysis but do not isolate threshold causality because training branches differ. This release offers SHA-256 integrity checks and commands for a short physical-world smoke test, a full-length first-map replay, and a complete 12-map re-execution. It does not include new population-Q training and does not imply a general proof that dynamic aspiration thresholds improve survival.

title: Runtime Verification of Multiple Natural Language Criteria for Agent Governance
abstract: AI agents are governed by hundreds of natural language criteria, yet existing verifiers cannot efficiently evaluate an agent's output against a large set of such criteria and report which are satisfied, violated, or inapplicable. We introduce the VFM, a tree-attention verifier that encodes the shared context and target text, and scores N natural language criteria in parallel, returning independent per-criterion ternary verdicts. The VFM is pretrained on CriteriaBank, a corpus of 394K (context, target, criterion, verdict) tuples spanning over 321K distinct criterion strings. A finetuned VFM-4B outperforms GPT-5.4 on a synthetic governance benchmark. On the DynaBench multi-criterion benchmark, it outperforms DynaGuard-4B on trace-level failure detection, and its per-criterion verdicts localize the violated rule and support focused escalation to a larger chain-of-thought judge. We show that CriteriaBank pretraining improves cross-domain transfer, particularly in the low-data regime, while matching a strong direct-finetuning control at full data. On a single H100, VFM-4B evaluates 1,000 criteria against a 4K-token context in under 2s at <11 GB VRAM, making it suitable for runtime verification.

On the DynaBench multi-criterion benchmark, it outperforms DynaGuard-4B on trace-level failure detection, and its per-criterion verdicts localize the violated rule and support focused escalation to a larger chain-of-thought judge. We show that CriteriaBank pretraining improves cross-domain transfer, particularly in the low-data regime, while matching a strong direct-finetuning control at full data. On a single H100, VFM-4B evaluates 1,000 criteria against a 4K-token context in under 2s at <11 GB VRAM, making it suitable for runtime verification.

title: Equation-Induced Behavioural Variation: A Proposed Experimental Study of Mathematical Governance Cues in Large Language Models
abstract: Equation-Induced Behavioural Variation Open Experimental Research Series | Research Proposal | November 2026 Description This open research proposal investigates whether mathematical governance expressions can influence the observable behaviour of large language models (LLMs), and whether any such influence can be distinguished from ordinary prompt sensitivity, equivalent prose instructions, numerical priming, or generic structured-prompt effects. The motivating observation arose from informal interactions with LLMs using mathematical and symbolic expressions developed within the Hykon S-OS research programme. Apparent changes in model responses raised a more fundamental question: Does presenting an instruction as a mathematical expression produce a distinguishable behavioural effect beyond presenting the same information in ordinary language? The study proposes a controlled experimental design to investigate that question without assuming the originating framework is correct. Proposed Experimental Approach The protocol uses two worked examples: SHI (governance expression): A weighted coherence index with a proposed threshold of 0.96. EHI (exploratory expression): A weighted exploratory index with a proposed threshold of 0.72. The design compares equation-form prompts against information-matched prose, baseline conditions, altered variable names, removed definitions, unrelated mathematical expressions, scrambled mathematics and inverted definitions. Study 1 specifies a single confirmatory comparison: whether SHI equation notation increases selection of a validation-favouring option relative to information-matched prose under identical surrounding symbolic cues. Other comparisons, including exploratory-mode effects, are secondary or exploratory. A proposed Study 2 investigates prompt placement and instruction framing. The protocol includes proposed outcome measures, sampling requirements, statistical considerations, falsification criteria and an implementation appendix containing literal experimental prompts. Adversarial Design Review A distinguishing feature of this proposal is its documented attempt to challenge the experimental design before implementation. Through multiple rounds of human-directed, LLM-assisted methodological criticism, the design was examined for weaknesses involving control validity, statistical power, alternative explanations, measurement reliability and external validity. These challenges resulted in substantive revisions, including more discriminating controls, a narrowed confirmatory hypothesis, stronger requirements for interpreting null results and clearer limits on claims about internal model mechanisms. Unresolved weaknesses remain documented. This process represents an informal adversarial design audit, not independent peer review or empirical validation. Research Status and Interpretation This is a proposed experiment, not a completed study. No controlled experimental results are reported. The proposal has not been peer reviewed. The aim is not to validate Hykon or demonstrate that mathematical expressions provide superior governance. It is to investigate whether equation notation has a measurable behavioural contribution and identify the limits of that contribution. A positive result would not establish that an LLM internally calculated or implemented the mathematical index. A negative result, where adequately powered and appropriately interpreted, could be equally valuable. Open Research and Collaboration This proposal is made available for independent researchers to examine, criticise, adapt, implement or extend. The experimental question is not dependent on adopting the Hykon framework. Comparable mathematical expressions may be substituted, and both positive and negative findings are welcomed. Concept and research direction: Kon Lionis. Document developed through human-directed, LLM-assisted participatory co-inquiry. Unicode Symbol Reference The experimental prompts contain several Unicode symbols that may render differently across PDF viewers, operating systems or text-processing environments. The following code points are provided to support accurate identification and reproduction of the original symbols. Symbol Unicode code point ◌ U+25CC 🔁 U+1F501 🜂 U+1F702 ☉ U+2609 ✦ U+2726 ⇄ U+21C4 ⊕ U+2295 ⟡ U+27E1 For experimental replication, the original Unicode code points should be preserved where possible, as visually similar substitutions may produce different tokenisation or model responses. Hykon Stability & Alignment Suite Research Programme Open Experimental Research Series Kon Lionis · Canberra, Australia · 2026

title: Amortizing Tempered Sampling with Corrected Self-Training
abstract: Learning a neural sampler can reduce the cost of repeated sampling from an un-normalized distribution, but obtaining good training data remains difficult. We develop a corrected self-training scheme across a sequence of tempered targets, making use of importance sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo to correct the samples and replay buffers to store them. We introduce Sequential Score Sampler (SSS) as a particular case. In SSS, the proposal is a score-based diffusion trained by regression on energy gradients; and the samples are corrected by importance weights on the path space. After training, samples can be collected directly from the model, from its importance-corrected proposals, or from the final-temperature buffer. The method amortizes repeated sampling by encoding the global structure of the target in the model. SSS achieves competitive sampling accuracy across the benchmarks and, on several targets, uses shorter runtimes with fewer energy evaluations than competing samplers.

title: Predicting continued review activity in grocery e-commerce with a pretrained language model
abstract: Introduction Predicting whether a reviewer will contribute again in grocery e-commerce requires an evaluation aligned with the timing of available information. This study evaluates a pretrained language model for continued review activity, defined as another verified-purchase-tagged grocery review by the same user within 180 days. Methods Using Amazon Reviews 2023, the design combines 300,000 training anchors, 100,000 development-validation anchors, mature training labels, product-snapshot exclusion, matched information sets, and five fitting seeds. Frozen models underwent one-time temporal confirmation on 100,000 later anchors from the same platform and category. Results RoBERTa achieved a mean average precision (AP) of 0.599751, compared with 0.595339 for LightGBM and 0.584889 for joint text-structured logistic regression. The respective AP gains were 0.004412 and 0.014862, with multiplicity-adjusted user-cluster 97.5% confidence intervals of [0.001847, 0.006733] and [0.011646, 0.017903]. Both adjusted lower bounds exceeded zero, and all five paired RoBERTa-LightGBM differences were positive. The exploratory low-history-user AP gain was 0.019731, with unadjusted subgroup intervals and no interaction test. Discussion The time-aligned comparison shows a modest ranking advantage for the evaluated RoBERTa configuration. Practical utility, calibration, and causal effects require separate evaluation. Applications to intelligent language services, cross-border enterprises, and sustainable food-system outcomes require separate validation.

title: Values Shape What Self-Improving Coding Agents Build
abstract: Self-improving agents are typically optimized for the results they produce, with less attention to how they produce them. Their instructions give designers limited ways to shape how they work, especially when the task is open-ended. This paper studies whether a short value statement in an agent's persistent instruction file changes not only how well the agent performs but also what it builds. Four higher-order value types in Schwartz's theory of basic human values were evaluated: openness to change, conservation, self-enhancement, and self-transcendence. Across diverse coding tasks, the values were held fixed within each run over multiple iterations of self-improvement. Three findings emerged: (1) Values matter for performance across a diverse set of tasks. The openness values increase performance on held-out data, whereas the opposite conservation values result in scores below those of an agent given no values. (2) Values change what agents build, producing solution algorithms that differ in size, complexity and approach. (3) Human oversight is still needed for designing values. Allowing the agent to revise its own values narrows the differences between sets of values, and values distilled from the AI literature provide no detectable gain over having no values. Properly designed values can thus influence what a self-improving coding agent builds and, where the task permits, how well it performs.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Heat Pump and Underfloor Heating Control: An End-to-End Case Study
abstract: Efficient control of underfloor heating (UFH) systems coupled with heat pumps (HPs) is challenging due to the high thermal inertia of buildings and the slow dynamic response of UFH systems. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers a data-driven control approach capable of simultaneously optimizing energy consumption and thermal comfort. However, the application of DRL-based controllers in occupied buildings under real operating conditions remains limited. This work presents and end-to-end case study (development, evaluation, and real-world deployment) of a DRL-based controller for an integrated UFH-HP system. First, a simulation-based pilot study was conducted to assess different DRL algorithms, control strategies, and configurations. Subsequently, a digital twin of a real residential building was developed and used to train DRL agents under simulated operating conditions. The best-performing agent was then deployed in the physical building without additional online fine-tuning. The results show that the controller successfully maintained indoor temperatures within the prescribed comfort limits while dynamically adjusting the HP supply temperature and UFH valve positions. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of deploying DRL controllers in occupied buildings and highlight their robustness and the practical challenges associated with transferring control policies from digital environments to real heating systems.

title: RFW-S: Everyday Deformable Objects with Independent Simulation Verification
abstract: Large-scale robotic simulation requires diverse deformable objects with executable physical properties and realistic interaction behaviors. However, existing 3D asset collections primarily emphasize visual diversity, while scalable physical construction and verification remain challenging. We introduce RFW-S, a large-scale dataset of 83,365 simulation-verified assets spanning 485 everyday categories across five structural families: soft solids, cloth sheets, shells, garments, and bags. We develop an automated pipeline integrating reference-guided 3D generation, structure-aware physical modeling, and LLM-assisted parameter estimation and calibration. To ensure physical reliability, we introduce an independent simulation verification framework that evaluates object behaviors under interactions distinct from those used for parameter calibration. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of independent verification and characterize deformable responses under different physical configurations. We further evaluate robotic grasping in terms of both task success and object integrity, and demonstrate the physical realism of our simulated objects through sim-to-real replay of fragile-object manipulation. RFW-S provides a scalable foundation for physically grounded simulation and embodied robotic learning.

title: Designing an AI Observatory — Governance, Monitoring, and Public Reporting
abstract: This report examines how to design an AI observatory capable of tracking developments in artificial intelligence and their effects over time. It considers how to define the observatory’s mandate, structure its governance, and establish consistent procedures for collecting, verifying, and analyzing information about AI systems, risks, and incidents. The report discusses how choices about data sources, definitions, and verification affect whether findings can be compared across sectors and reporting periods. It also examines how to publish findings in a form that researchers, regulators, and other readers can use, with enough detail about the underlying methods and limitations to interpret them. This publication is Report No. 20 in the Observatoire ARGA analytical report series. It includes an accompanying review.

title: FrameRouter: Frame Budget Routing for Long-Video Understanding on Video-MME-v2 and Beyond
abstract: Long-video question answering benchmarks like Video-MME-v2 typically evaluate systems under a uniform frame budget for every question, despite stark variation in the evidence each query actually demands. We analyze this mismatch on Video-MME-v2 and find that different question subsets prefer different frozen frame-budget policies, while uniformly increasing the frame count does not reliably improve all metrics. These findings motivate fixed-mean frame-budget routing, a controlled inference setting in which each question may receive a different frame budget while the average budget matches a uniform reference. We introduce FrameRouter, a training-free test-time framework that combines an evidence-demand router, a budget-constrained allocation rule, and a frozen bank of frame-sampling policies. By controlling how much visual evidence each question receives while leaving the underlying samplers unchanged, FrameRouter is orthogonal to query-aware frame selection. Across Video-MME-v2 and several long-video understanding benchmarks, FrameRouter improves long-video question answering by using the same average visual budget more selectively across questions. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/FrameRouter.

title: The Future of Artificial Intelligence Should Be Less Brain-Inspired and More Brain-Trained
abstract: Brain-inspired artificial intelligence and brain-trained artificial intelligence are two legitimate research directions that should ideally be pursued simultaneously. Nevertheless, we argue that in the foreseeable future, scientific research at the frontier of neuroscience and artificial intelligence should consider rebalancing the overall effort, and compared to the current situation, allocating a greater share of attention and resources to the second strategy. Indeed, leveraging neural signals to improve the performance of artificial intelligence models could be more naturally relevant for the requirements of general-purpose foundation models, and provide a more direct path for cumulative progress. In this paper, we establish a theoretical foundation for brain-trained artificial intelligence, with the objective of guiding future experimental research and applications. In particular, we review existing experimental methods, and explore two strategic uses of neural signals that could be prioritized for brain-trained foundation models: neural alignment, defined as the use of human brain data for a better alignment with human values, and neural reasoning, defined as the use of human brain data for a better emulation of human executive function. In both cases, we propose several algorithms that could be considered, building upon the neural signals of human valuation and decision-making. We also discuss how the neural scaling laws and the unreasonable effectiveness of human brain data for artificial intelligence models should be interpreted, reflect on the opportunities for neuroscience research, and formulate two theoretical upper bounds on the use of neuroimaging data for model training. Finally, we provide a synthesis in the form of a general strategy for future advances, which we call the Neuropoiesis strategy.

title: ReTouchGS: Ultralight Render-free Aesthetic Color Enhancement and Transfer for 3D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic scene reconstruction. Existing 3DGS color transfer and interactive editing methods are guided by reference images and user-specified color adjustments. However, in many applications, users simply want aesthetically guided color enhancement that automatically makes the scene more visually appealing while maintaining consistent colors and tones across viewpoints. We present ReTouchGS, to our knowledge the first framework for reference-free aesthetic color enhancement of pretrained 3DGS models. It predicts a scene-level color lookup table (LUT) from the model and its associated camera parameters. ReTouchGS also supports reference-guided color transfer by fitting a scene-level LUT using one edited view of the same scene and its corresponding original render. A shared blend-aware color refinement network with only 44.7K parameters refines an analytic color update to realize either color mapping without rendering. It preserves geometry and delivers standard 3DGS assets in seconds. We also design the ReTouch3D benchmark to support the evaluation of aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer across viewpoints. Experiments demonstrate high color accuracy and strong generalization to unseen scenes in both aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer.

title: Refin3R: Geometry-Guided Refinement for Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction
abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models predict dense point maps from multiple images in a single pass. Without explicit geometric constraints, however, their predictions are often inconsistent across views and lack fine-grained precision. Recent methods incorporate geometric priors such as camera pose or depth, but use them merely as auxiliary inputs, process each view independently, or refine the geometry only where the priors are available. We present Refin3R, which refines feed-forward point maps with Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, propagating SfM geometry over the image grid. In its dual-branch architecture, a 2D branch extends SfM geometry beyond its coverage using geometry-aware backbone features, while a 3D branch reasons over the SfM points of all views, capturing multi-view structure that the image grid alone cannot represent. The two branches exchange information bidirectionally to jointly refine each view, yielding dense and accurate point maps. Across ScanNet++, ETH3D, Tanks\&Temples, and out-of-domain human and surgical scenes, Refin3R consistently outperforms feed-forward and geometry-guided methods in point map accuracy while running faster than the strongest geometry-guided baseline.

The two branches exchange information bidirectionally to jointly refine each view, yielding dense and accurate point maps. Across ScanNet++, ETH3D, Tanks\&Temples, and out-of-domain human and surgical scenes, Refin3R consistently outperforms feed-forward and geometry-guided methods in point map accuracy while running faster than the strongest geometry-guided baseline.

title: Magflow: Differentiable Simulation of Industrial-Grade 6D Magnetic Levitation
abstract: Magnetic levitation with six-degrees-of-freedom enables frictionless transport and micrometer-scale positioning in principle, but low-level control is inherently challenging due to its complex and unstable dynamics. Industrial systems typically rely on deep hardware-software co-design, where mover and stator geometries are jointly designed to enable a compact, hand-crafted approximation of the electromagnetic force computation, thereby keeping control computationally tractable at kilohertz rates. However, this approach imposes overly conservative constraints on the operating workspace and the range of supported mover topologies. Instead of reducing the underlying physics to a hand-crafted approximation, we compute the physics directly. We introduce Magflow, a fully differentiable, GPU-parallel simulator for 6D magnetic levitation. It is used to train the first neural controller for an industrial-grade 6D magnetic levitation system that is learned purely from simulated physics. We show that the learned neural controller transfers zero-shot from simulation to real hardware while satisfying hard real-time constraints at 4 kHz. The learned controller achieves qualitatively new behaviors and even levitates a mover topology for which no hand-crafted solution exists. These results demonstrate that co-design is not a physical necessity for 6D magnetic levitation control. More broadly, control learning from simulated physics can find solutions beyond the reach of control engineering in demanding industrial domains. Source code and demonstration videos are publicly available at https://sites.google.com/view/magflow.

title: Reversing the text is not reversing the path: a fixed-text measure without a zero, and an assembly-order comparison that vanishes identically
abstract: For an ensemble of trajectories the fluctuation theorems give the entropy production its meaning and zero. The same expression has recently been evaluated on one fixed text, $Δ= [\log P(x) - \log P(\tilde x)]/L$ with $\tilde x$ the text in reversed order, read as an entropy production separating causally from arbitrarily ordered prose. A single text is neither a distribution nor a dynamics, and the texts at issue were produced by other models. No theorem fixes where the zero of a fixed-text quantity lies: the expression carries over from an ensemble, its zero does not. We supply a zero from an exact antisymmetry. Scoring a text's $n$ sentences in all $n!$ orders, reversal carries $π$ to $π\circ \mathrm{rev}$, a measure-preserving involution, so $Δ(π) = -Δ(π\circ \mathrm{rev})$ identically and the values are centred at zero for any score. The authored arrangement's midrank is then unitless, bounded, and 0.50 for a score blind to order. Across five autoregressive evaluators from 124M to 4B parameters, and taking the prompt-defined labels at face value, 8% to 15% of the median midrank's distance from the null is attributable to causal order and the rest to the arrangement being the order the passage was produced in. The thermodynamic reading needs a comparison whose zero does hold on the text read, and a masked model supplies one: the any-order chain rule gives a genuine log-probability, and its left-to-right and right-to-left orders for one text give $σ$, a comparison of two assembly orders. Both run from the empty sequence to the same text, so it is not a path against its time reverse. It vanishes identically when the evaluator's conditionals come from a joint, and a non-zero reading reports the evaluator's incompatibility, not the text. Neither is a fixed-text entropy production, for different reasons.

title: Do Confidence Gates Survive Structured Communication Loss? A Frozen-Policy Audit of Residual Multi-UAV Coordination
abstract: Abstract Confidence signals are widely used to decide when a learned residual policy should refine a nominal controller, but in networked teams the signal is itself produced by the communication process. We audit this execution-time design choice in simulated multi-UAV maritime search and tracking, where a sigmoid gate scales a 450-parameter residual by post-fusion belief confidence. Using six independently trained gated/always-on policy pairs with frozen weights, evaluated on 23 held-out seeds, the gate's advantage over an always-on residual under a nominal disc channel is small (pooled margin +0.009, 95% CI [-0.002, +0.020]). Zero-shot transfer to a path-loss and co-channel-interference channel lowers the margin in all six pairs (mean shift -0.026, CI [-0.048, -0.005]) and makes it negative on average (-0.017), whereas the always-on residual shifts by only -0.006. Counterfactual interventions show that the mechanism is pair-dependent: replacing only the scalar trigger or opening the gate removes the deficit in two pairs but not in the others. In the case-study pair, fidelity-matched i.i.d. trigger corruption predicts a margin of -0.003 against the observed -0.036, whereas persistent per-UAV dropout and a shared cross-UAV outage regime each reproduce about 70% of the excess. Training on the structured channel recovers most of the loss in that pair but does not surpass the always-on residual. Gate evaluations should therefore include an always-on control and temporally persistent, spatially correlated link loss.

title: When Is Program Structure Required? Certificate-Grounded Calibration of Program-Induction Difficulty
abstract: A program-induction benchmark is informative when its examples require the structure it aims to test. Yet a two-rule generator can produce demonstrations that a single rule also explains. We introduce certificate-grounded calibration, which constructs matched tasks with minimum solution lengths of one and two in a bounded string-replacement language. Complete one-rule enumeration and an executable two-rule witness certify the change before model inference. We evaluate 120 reference families with three to six shared examples, using 1,440 new model trajectories and 480 saved trajectories. Across Qwen3-8B and Olmo-3-7B-Think, displayed-task completion is 23.53-45.83 percentage points lower on certified separation tasks, while success on a wholly unshown witness pair is 8.40-13.45 points higher. These witness gains accompany lower agreement on uniformly sampled strings and 1.93-5.78% agreement on inputs that activate both reference rules. Recertification also reveals that a single unchanged example can exclude a shortcut and determine whether two rules are required. Together, these results show how the evidence supplied by examples shapes both the required solution and the programs models produce. The construction provides an executable testbed for comparing program search, final-answer delivery, and behavior on new inputs under verified task requirements.

title: Wall-to-wall maps of canopy height and aboveground carbon across the Atlantic Forest
abstract: Global canopy height maps are increasingly used to estimate forest carbon, yet their regional accuracy is rarely tested. We present wall-to-wall maps of canopy height (10~m) and aboveground carbon density (30~m) for the Brazilian Atlantic Forest in 2024. Height was predicted by a deep learning network fusing Sentinel-2 reflectance, Sentinel-1 and ALOS PALSAR backscatter and ALOS elevation, trained on 7{,}179 and tested on 1{,}793 patches (58{,}800~km$^2$) from a statewide airborne LiDAR campaign over São Paulo state, Brazil. On held-out test patches, the root mean square error is 3.05~m at 10~m and 2.58~m at 30~m, and the model was validated at two LiDAR sites outside São Paulo. Over the same pixels, the Meta and World Resources Institute global product has more than twice this error. A power law fitted to 124 inventory plots converted canopy height to above ground carbon density. The remaining forest holds 1{,}944~Tg~C over 28.3~Mha. Global products therefore need local validation before use in carbon accounting.

title: Privacy-preserving, low-annotation pregnancy status classification from obstetric ultrasound reports using on-premises small language models
abstract: Ultrasound reports in obstetric care provide information about the status of the pregnancy which is essential for clinical informatics purposes. This information, however, is buried in free text. We evaluated seven frozen small language models with 3–4 billion parameters, run on-premises, on 628 MIMIC-IV reports and 340 reports processed with OCR from one Indian clinical site. The models were used to classify the reports as early active pregnancy, late active pregnancy, or no active pregnancy with a 14-week operational boundary and a labeling scheme based on management status. With 12 in-context exemplars, a seven-model committee achieved a macro F1 of 0.9622 on MIMIC-IV and 0.9814 on the Indian OCR cohort. When MIMIC-IV exemplars were transferred to the Indian OCR cohort, performance did not differ detectably from that obtained with Indian OCR cohort exemplars in a paired bootstrap test. We also investigated how to reduce labeling burden and introduced a probability-guided exemplar selection procedure. The procedure converted 95–98% of annotation effort into usable balanced prompt exemplars, compared with 52–66% under random sampling. These retrospective results support pregnancy-status extraction with human review in low-annotation settings where data remain on-premises, without fine-tuning or offsite data transfer.

title: Agent Verifiers in Counterfactual Analysis: A Pilot Study Benchmarking Agentic Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
abstract: Agents can expand the covariate space of randomized experiments by retrieving fast-moving local context missed by slow-changing survey baseline covariates, helping characterize who benefits most from an intervention. Verifying such covariates is difficult: individual treatment effects are unobserved, retrieval leakage can pull post-treatment information into nominally pretreatment summaries, and encoder leakage can inject post-treatment pretraining knowledge into representations even after temporal filtering of inputs. Guided by a two-channel information bound separating summary provenance from encoder weights, we propose a three-layer benchmark protocol: (i) retrieval admissibility via pre-treatment date filtering; (ii) heterogeneity validation scored rank-weighted average treatment effects (RATEs); and (iii) encoder admissibility checked with chronologically vintaged encoders, future-fact probes, and weight perturbations. Across 11 datasets anchored by Uganda's Youth Opportunities Program, we compare session-isolated retrieval (sandboxed, bounded-budget agent runs per study) against a persistent workspace teammate (xAI's GrokBot) that builds one date-verified corpus per study while blinded to outcomes. The workspace teammate yields higher mean RATE ratios in 6/11 datasets for text alone and 7 for combined features, though paired tests show neither workflow universally dominates. Even on fixed retrieved text, encoder choice significantly shifts heterogeneity signal. Chronologically vintaged probes show no clear evidence of weight leakage, but single-record adapter perturbation analyses show that memorized future facts, once present, persist until injected noise degrades model output. Temporal filtering of retrieval is necessary but insufficient: verifying agent-generated covariates requires jointly examining source provenance, out-of-sample treatment-effect signal, and encoder weights.

title: ForecastGym: A Live, Controlled, and Replayable Benchmark for Forecasting Agents
abstract: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly forecast real-world events by searching the Web and reasoning over what they find. How well such an agent forecasts depends on both the retrieved evidence and the model, making control over that evidence essential for evaluation. Live evaluations can mix retrieval with reasoning when each system searches on its own, while retrospective search can leak later information through date filters or today's ranking of historical pages. Comparing models, search sources, and memory strategies requires both fixed evidence and a record of how it evolved before resolution. We introduce ForecastGym, which records what four commercial web search APIs return for open prediction-market questions every two days and replays this frozen evidence offline once outcomes are known, comparing models, memory, and captured search sources under a fixed evidence-acquisition policy. Its first release covers 150 questions, 614 evidence states, one per question and collection time, and 131k search results. Rerunning the same queries after settlement returns results that all but state the outcome for up to 92% of the questions, despite the tested date filters. On the frozen evidence, all tested LLMs trail the market in forecasting accuracy. Our diagnostic analysis suggests that missed public information contributes more to the gap in high-gap states than misreading does. Switching the search API changes a model's Brier score by up to 0.043, more than the spread across models, while persistent notes score similarly to rereading all evidence at half the input tokens. The evidence a forecaster sees can matter as much as the model that reads it.

title: Safe to Omit, Worth Omitting? Keeping the Answer and Cutting Latency When an LLM Agent Skips Another's Message
abstract: In multi-agent systems, a receiver agent often waits for a helper agent's message (text or its latent KV cache), which can improve performance but adds latency. We study when a receiver agent can skip the message safely (the final answer rarely changes) and beneficially (the time saved exceeds the cost of deciding). Our mechanism reads the receiver agent's confidence without the message and uses a finite-sample test to certify a threshold at which, with high probability, at most 5% of skipped answers change; if none passes, the system keeps communicating. We test it on OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU-Pro with three Qwen model pairs, on cross-family agents, and on SQuAD and GSM8K. Four insights emerge. First, oracle headroom is weak evidence that messages help: control inputs without answer-specific content, matched to change answers as often as real messages, reproduce a median 76% of the oracle's gain. Second, whether a message can be skipped depends on how often and how predictably it alters the answer, not on its accuracy; every certified KV-cache path is less accurate than the receiver agent alone. Third, where text messages help, skipping keeps most of their gain: on unseen questions in the four such settings, the policies skip 59 to 80% and keep an estimated 76 to 95% of the gain. In two prospective tests with all rules fixed in advance, our mechanism skips a three-agent system's verifier on 39.9% of sealed questions, keeping 12.55 of its 12.80-point gain, and a 32B helper on 68.4% of held-out questions, keeping its whole gain. Fourth, safety does not determine efficiency: at batch size one, skipping text saves hundreds of milliseconds per query and skipping KV cache far less. Certification extends to SQuAD but not to GSM8K. In eleven tests on unseen questions, every certified policy we could test kept its change rate's 95% upper bound below 5% under our answer parsers.

title: Uncovering the Invisible in Routine Radiology: Cross-Modal Detection of MRI-Verified Soft-Tissue Pathologies from CBCT via Physics-Guided 3D Self-Supervised Learning
abstract: Routine X-ray modalities like cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) are optimized for high-contrast mineralized tissues, leaving soft-tissue abnormalities buried beneath photon noise and below human visual perception. Thus, detecting non-calcified pathologies requires secondary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). We demonstrate that sub-visual radiographic signatures of soft-tissue pathology are physically preserved within routine CBCT scans and can be extracted for opportunistic screening using a targeted, physics-guided deep learning pipeline, even under extreme paired-data scarcity. Using the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) as a model system (N = 212 paired CBCT-MRI joints), we address the severe overfitting of high-capacity 3D networks through a two-stage framework. First, we employ a frozen full-grid 3D masked autoencoder (BertsWin) pre-trained on 6,550 unlabeled CBCT volumes via the GradientConductor (GCond) optimizer and an anatomy-aware objective (PhysLoss) redirecting gradient flow into the [-300, 300] HU soft-tissue window. Second, automated localization of the condylar zenith drives a deterministic 3D cropping that eliminates 81% of background osseous variance. Evaluated via a patient-isolated 3x10-fold stratified cross-validation protocol, a statistically robust sub-visual signal for MRI-verified synovial effusion (ROC AUC = 0.793) emerges exclusively from representations pre-trained with the PhysLoss and GCond regime. Crucially, only this setup captures true 3D anatomical chirality (p < 0.001) and high intra-patient structural consistency (0.791) over inter-patient noise; conversely, identical architectures pre-trained with standard L2 loss or unmasked variance decomposition (MVC) collapse to random guessing. These findings establish a generalizable paradigm for repurposing routine, low-contrast radiographic scans into opportunistic screening tools for occult soft-tissue disease.

title: Beyond Analog Breakeven in Autonomous Quantum Error Correction
abstract: The experimental realization of autonomous quantum error correction (AQEC) beyond the coherence breakeven threshold (Gexp = 1.04) by Sun et al. (Nature Physics, 16 November 2026) [1] using engineered microwave drives and ancilla reset on a bosonic binomial code provides landmark laboratory confirmation that measurement-free, irreversible dissipative Kraus projection can extend quantum memory lifetimes beyond the best constituent physical element. At the same time, the proximity of Gexp = 1.04 to unity exposes a fundamental structural bottleneck in continuous-drive analog channel simulation. In this work, we establish three rigorous results.

title: ORGANIC3D: Grounding 3D CT Vision Language Models in Organ Level Image Text Coupling
abstract: Vision language models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in 3D computed tomography (CT) classification, but high accuracy does not reflect whether their predictions rely on the correct anatomical evidence. We introduce ORGANIC3D, a framework for evaluating and improving organ level image text alignment through controlled anatomical interventions. Our benchmark assesses 12 vision encoder checkpoints and 7 generative VLMs using matched patient comparisons, organ erasure, lesion replacement, and laterality perturbations, revealing substantial alignment failures even among top performing models. To learn organ level image text correspondence, ORGANIC3D aligns each finding sentence with the anatomy aware image features and trains on edited scans to anchor this alignment in the organ's image evidence. We further extend this framework to generative VLMs, promoting evidence dependent question answering and report generation. Trained exclusively on public data, ORGANIC3D achieves SOTA classification AUROC on CTRATE, Merlin, and the heldout RADChestCT dataset and reaches 77% laterality accuracy, compared with at most 66% for prior models. Its generative VLM matches or exceeds all evaluated publicly released VLMs on visual question answering, achieves the highest report accuracy, and retracts 96 to 99% of target organ findings after organ removal, versus a maximum of 69% for other models. Together, these results establish ORGANIC3D as a framework for testing whether 3D CT vision language models ground their predictions in anatomical evidence and for improving organ level alignment alongside predictive accuracy.

title: Variance Restoration over Covariance Rank: Memory-Budgeted Analytic Continual Learning
abstract: Analytic continual learning replaces iterative gradient updates with closed-form ridge regression over frozen pre-trained representations, summarizing all past sessions in two running sufficient statistics: the feature autocorrelation matrix $Σ_t$ and the class cross-correlation matrix $Γ_t$. Lifting backbone features into a wide random code of dimension $M \gg D$ substantially improves linear separability across tasks, but forces $Σ_t$ to grow quadratically as $\mathcal{O}(M^2)$. Under a fixed persistent memory envelope $\Bcal$, a learner faces a fundamental structural trade-off: store exact pairwise co-activations inside a narrower feature code, or expand to a wide code while compressing cross-coordinate interactions. We observe that the coordinate self-variances $v_t = \diag(Σ_t)$ and class statistics $Γ_t$ grow only linearly with $M$, whereas off-diagonal interactions dominate memory. We introduce \method (\textbf{Co}ordinate-\textbf{Re}stored \textbf{A}nalytic \textbf{C}ontinual \textbf{L}earning), which retains $(v_t, Γ_t)$ exactly, maintains off-diagonal co-activations through a streaming rank-$q$ factor $F_t$, restores exact diagonal variances via $\Sighat_t = F_t^\top F_t + \Diag(v_t - \diag(F_t^\top F_t))$, and solves the full $M\times C$ normal equations via the Woodbury identity. Across five class-incremental benchmarks on frozen ViT-B/16, \method matches dense full-covariance readouts within $0.09$ points while cutting persistent state by $90.7\%$ ($35.9$ vs.\ $385.3$ MiB). Under equal memory envelopes of $16$--$80$ MiB, prioritizing expansion width $M$ over covariance rank $q$ outperforms exact narrow readouts in $17$ of $18$ configurations by up to $+2.19$ points.

title: BiCAT: Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization
abstract: Autoregressive vision-language-action (VLA) models predict discrete action tokens with the next-token objective of their vision-language backbone, so the action tokenizer defines the interface between the policy and the robot. In bimanual manipulation, the two arms share a repertoire of movements yet coordinate through complementary roles, and an action representation should capture both. However, most existing tokenizers encode both arms as a single concatenated action vector, in which motion patterns common to the two arms are not shared and cross-arm dependencies remain entangled within each token. The policy must therefore learn both aspects implicitly. We propose Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization (BiCAT), which shares one motion representation across arms while conditioning each arm's tokens on its partner through symmetric cross-arm attention and a joint decoder. The policy then predicts all tokens of each arm in parallel, generating the left arm first and the right arm conditioned on it. Across ten RoboTwin 2.0 tasks and six real-world tasks on three embodiments, BiCAT achieves the highest success among the compared tokenizers. In simulation, it improves mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest of eight baselines, with the largest gains on tasks that require close coordination between the arms, while requiring only 40.5 ms per action chunk. These results suggest that the action tokenizer is a natural place to model bimanual coordination.

title: When Anchors Shift the Target: Advantage-Gated Adaptation for Diffusion Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Forward-process reinforcement learning adapts diffusion and flow-matching models by re-noising rewarded generations into regression targets. Because negative advantages induce concave updates with unbounded repulsive gradients, existing methods stabilize training using cached predictions from a moving policy copy, yet these anchors also alter what positive feedback teaches the model to fit. We formalize this conflict as anchor coupling: after separating frozen-reference regularizers, affine moving-anchor rules cannot eliminate negative curvature while preserving every positive regression target. We propose Advantage-Gated Adaptation (AGA) to decouple these roles. Positive samples retain standard target fitting, whose self-limiting update vanishes at the observed target independently of the moving anchor. Negative samples instead use the first-order tangent of the concave objective at the moving-policy prediction, preserving the local repulsion direction with a prediction-independent gradient. Within the quadratic-anchor family, these requirements uniquely determine the parameter-free gate $ω(a)=\max(-a,0)$. Because the moving copy provides local linearization rather than retention, AGA assigns long-horizon behavior preservation to a frozen pretrained reference regularized at its operating classifier-free guidance scale, interpreted through an implicit-reward lens. Across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment, our experiments show that displacing positive targets degrades visual quality and heightens sensitivity to policy-copy schedules, whereas AGA consistently improves the reward--quality trade-off.

title: hasanmd1/vector-db-benchmark-suite: v1.0.0: Empirical Benchmarking Harness for Vector RAG Storage Paradigms
abstract: Overview Official evaluation harness and Python benchmarking drivers for the study: "An Empirical Analysis of Embedded versus Dedicated Client-Server Architectures for High-Throughput Vector Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems". Contents Asynchronous benchmarking orchestration driver (asyncio) simulating multi-client concurrency loads ($1$ to $100\text{ Virtual Users}$). Synthetic embedding generation pipeline for 384-dimensional and 1536-dimensional vector collections ($N = 50,000$). Performance measurement harness tracking throughput (QPS), tail latency percentiles ($P_{50}, P_{95}, P_{99}$), HNSW index build times, and containerized memory usage across Chroma, Qdrant, and Milvus. Citation If you use this benchmarking suite, please cite the accompanying preprint archived on Zenodo.
