title: Construction Algorithm for Adaptive Morphological Structural Elements Based on Fuzzy C-Means Clustering with a Greyscale Fluctuation Factor
abstract: Conventional morphological operations commonly utilize a structural element with a single shape and fixed size for image processing. Due to the complexity and diversity of image targets, morphological operations using this structural element may lead to changes in the image target feature information. For example, the target boundary contours may be shifted, new artificial targets may appear, and target details may be lost. To address this, a morphological adaptive structural element construction method based on fuzzy C-means (FCM) is proposed. The constructed structural elements are able to change their shapes adaptively according to the edge features of the image target. First, a new FCM objective function is constructed utilizing the grey fluctuation factor to improve the homogeneity of pixel clustering. Then, using the objective function and incorporating the density peaking (DP) algorithm, a local subregion of the image is clustered. Finally, the boundary points between the classes after clustering are considered to be the adaptive structural elements of this subregion. The experimental results show that morphological operations on an image that adopt this adaptive structural element can obtain the adaptive structural element corresponding to the shape of the image target, maintain the integrity of the necessary information of the target, avoid a target boundary contour offset, and improve the accuracy of target boundary contour localization. In addition, this method effectively preserves the geometric structural properties of the image and reduces the distortion level of the target structural details of the image.

title: Where Global Context and Weight Sharing Work in Compact Vision Backbones
abstract: Compact convolutional backbones such as EfficientNet achieve strong parameter efficiency through local depthwise separable convolutions, yet two structural questions remain central to hybrid design: where does global self-attention improve recognition over pure convolution, and can repeated blocks share weights without losing representational capacity? We investigate both questions on ImageNet-1k (50,000-image validation) using controlled EfficientNet-B0 experiments. First, we show that wrapping a classification backbone in multi-scale feature pyramids (BiFPN) fails to outperform a plain MBConv trunk (69.99% - 71.81% vs. 72.86% plain B0) until paired with stage attention (73.15%). In contrast, keeping the MBConv trunk intact and inserting lightweight zero-gated residual self-attention adapters at stages P3 (28x28 windowed), P4 (14x14 global), and P5 (7x7 global) reaches 74.02% standalone and outperforms a bit-for-bit matched plain-B0 control by +0.954 percentage points (73.88% vs. 72.92%) across an 88-epoch stateless replay schedule, with learned attention amplitude rising monotonically with semantic depth (27.2% at P3 -> 45.4% at P4 -> 66.3% at P5). Second, we evaluate recurrent weight sharing across repeated MBConv blocks with pass-specific BatchNorm statistics (+1,536 parameters per pass). While post-hoc kernel averaging degrades accuracy to 17.03% and single-template stage tying (-27.6% parameters) plateaus at 66.10%, alternating two shared block templates ([B1, A, B, A]) in Stage 6 cuts total model parameters by 10.9% (582K weights) and recovers by +10.82 points in a single epoch to 70.92% (-1.84 points vs. unshared control).

title: Automated Annotation-Free Synthetic Data Generation for Underwater Litter Detection: A Comparison of Generative Approaches
abstract: Underwater object detection is often limited by scarce and imbalanced training data and by strong appearance variations caused by turbidity, lighting, and differences between sensors. Existing data augmentation strategies, such as geometric or color augmentation or fully synthetic image generation with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), either lack semantic realism, fail to respect scene physics, or require additional annotations. In low-data domains like underwater environmental monitoring, the need for additional annotations is often the core bottleneck. Collecting new footage is hard, but labeling this dataset is even more time-consuming and costly, which limits how quickly a usable dataset can be constructed. We propose a unified fully automated zero-annotation pipeline that inserts class-conditioned trash objects into real underwater frames while preserving the original background context. Starting from sampled bounding boxes, each box is converted into an insertion mask and the object is pasted or generated within it, while the same box coordinates are automatically written as the corresponding annotation. Because labels are derived directly from the sampled boxes, the pipeline generates fully labeled training data for low-data settings without any manual annotation. Within this single pipeline we compare three strategies: copy-paste, Stable Diffusion inpainting, and DALL-E image-conditioned generation. We evaluate bounding-box faithfulness, visual realism, and the impact of the generated samples on downstream detector performance on the SeaClear underwater debris dataset. Results show that DALL-E improves detection performance in four of five domains, with relative gains of up to 96 percent over the real-only baseline.

title: ADAPT-IQP
abstract: Code, Two Moons samples and results for the article "Gradient Blindness in Adaptive Architecture Search for IQP Born Machines". The package grows instantaneous quantum polynomial (IQP) Born machines adaptively by adding in every round the candidate gates with the largest loss gradient, starting from a seed of one-qubit gates or from one-qubit gates plus the edges of the Chow-Liu tree. It contains the training code (exact KL loss for Two Moons, MMD loss for Binary Blobs and the D-Wave dataset), the Hydra configurations of all circuits in the article, the per-round and per-step metrics of every run, and the data and sources of all figures. The Binary Blobs and D-Wave datasets are not included and are available from Recio-Armengol et al., "Train on classical, deploy on quantum" (2025).

title: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
abstract: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.

title: Storing the Gemma 4 K=V Cache Once: Exact Global-KV Memory Savings in a Paged Serving Engine with Unchanged Attention Kernels
abstract: In the global attention layers of Gemma 4 31B, the value is the normalized key projection, and the key is the value scaled by a fixed weight, with rotary position encoding on one quarter of its dimensions. The Gemma 4 report states that this design reduces the global KV cache by up to 37.5%, but the open serving engines that we checked still store a full key and a full value: 1,024 values per KV head and token. We store one 640-value row instead, exact in real arithmetic, and an unchanged paged attention kernel reads it through two overlapping strided views as its key cache and its value cache. In a vLLM prototype with the 16-bit 31B model, the outputs are bit-identical to an emulation of the same arithmetic on the stock cache, 2 of 432 final answers differ from the stock engine (within its run-to-run noise), and the steady decode KV memory per request falls by a factor of 1.34 to 1.40 at 32K to 64K tokens. On a prefill/decode pair of two A100 GPUs with NIXL transfer and CPU offload, a decode engine with a full 15 GiB pool ran 1.38 times the stock decode tokens per step for 16K-token prompts (repeated to 0.06%) and 1.24 times for 8K-token prompts; a model of the vLLM block pool predicted both ratios to within 1% (the engine was 0.7% to 0.9% higher) and matched the change between them. The eager decode throughput rose by 1.30 and 1.11 times, and on this path the compact engine gave the same output tokens as the emulation for 8 prompts at batch 1. The run-time prototype makes an eager step 4% to 9% slower at equal batch, and the method does not yet stack with an 8-bit KV cache at the default scale.

title: Quantum expectation value estimation by doubling the number of qubits
abstract: Expectation value estimation is ubiquitous in quantum algorithms. The expectation value of a Hamiltonian, which is essential in various practical applications, is often estimated by measuring a large number of Pauli strings on quantum computers and performing classical post-processing. In the case of $n$-qubit molecular Hamiltonians in quantum chemistry calculations, it is necessary to evaluate $O(n^4)$ Pauli strings, requiring a large number of measurements for accurate estimation. To reduce the measurement cost, we assess an existing idea that uses two copies of an $n$-qubit quantum state of interest and coherently measures them in the Bell basis, which enables the simultaneous estimation of the absolute values of expectation values of all the $n$-qubit Pauli strings. We numerically investigate the efficiency of energy estimation for molecular Hamiltonians of up to 12 qubits. The results show that, when the target precision is no smaller than tens of milli-Hartree, this method requires fewer measurements than conventional sampling methods. This suggests that the method may be useful for many applications that rely on expectation value estimation of Hamiltonians and other observables as well when moderate precision is sufficient.

title: Privacy-Cost Cooperative Games and Prefix-Sampling Data Valuation: An Adult Benchmark Study
abstract: We formulate a cooperative data-sharing game with task utility, a stylized privacy cost and a coordination charge. Convexity and approximate core guarantees require explicit net-worth and error conditions. Ordered prefix sampling exposes individual marginals through public differences; the experiment evaluates a simulated interface. On one Adult split with 400 valuation and 600 evaluation records, a kNN recursion reportedly agrees with eight-record enumeration to 6.9e-16. At 128 permutations, simulated SecPSA has Spearman agreement 0.564 ± 0.036 with the recursion anchor, versus 0.572 ± 0.032 for Monte Carlo and 0.605 ± 0.017 for Data Banzhaf. Matched-permutation vectors reportedly agree exactly, with 6–16% simulated overhead. Privacy costs and institutional coalitions remain untested. Original utility definitions, code and seed-level outputs are required to audit the larger-pool anchor and statistical summaries.

title: Autoregressive View Model
abstract: We present the Autoregressive View Model (AVM), which generates a scene as a stream of views without constructing an explicit 3D representation. Through a unified in-context interface, AVM conditions on images or videos to generate short clips along a requested camera path. Visual context grounds reconstruction and interpolation, while a learned prior enables extrapolation into unseen regions. AVM retrieves relevant views from inputs and generated history to form a bounded active context. We fine-tune a pretrained bidirectional video diffusion transformer with flow matching in an N-in-1-out formulation. We then tune a causal model on its own rollouts to improve photorealism, reduce denoising steps, and limit long-horizon drift. We scale training to approximately 8M scenes and video clips. We evaluate generation capacity and scene persistence across benchmarks for camera control, text control, visual quality, dynamics, sparse and 4D reconstruction, and long-horizon consistency. The results demonstrate that AVM adapts to diverse input and output settings through one in-context interface.

title: RFBench: A Simulator-Grounded Multimodal Benchmark for Passive RF Layout Design and Understanding
abstract: While multimodal language models can interpret diagrams and generate structured outputs, their capacity to connect passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior remains largely untested. To address this gap, we introduce RFBench, a simulator-grounded dataset and benchmark for passive RF layout design and understanding. The dataset contains 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, with each layout represented by editable geometric primitives, a raster image, a 16x16 occupancy grid, complex S-parameters at 201 frequency points, a structural category, and an RF response label. Building on these aligned representations, we define seven tasks spanning specification-conditioned layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator-based validation, design diagnosis and improvement, structural understanding, and response classification. Extensive baselines across seven multimodal language models reveal systematic weaknesses in generating structurally valid layouts and predicting electromagnetically faithful responses. We show that RF-specific fine-tuning increases T1a structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and the T3 primitive-input within-2-dB rate from 17.7% to 62.8%, demonstrating the value of domain adaptation while leaving considerable room for further progress. RFBench establishes a common testbed for evaluating multimodal RF capabilities and guiding the development of models that connect design intent and layout representations with physical behavior.

title: Check Your Blind Spots: Decision-Guided Perception by Probing the Planner with Hypothetical Objects
abstract: Not every perception error changes the planner's action. Yet adaptive-resolution perception chooses where to spend high-resolution computation from image cues, which can neither reliably point to an object that low resolution missed nor tell which objects matter to the planner. We observe that the planner can say where an object would matter before anything is seen: inserting a hypothetical object at a location tests whether its action would change. Decision-Guided Speculative Perception (DGSP) treats the low-resolution scene and its action as a draft and probes the planner in this way to obtain a decision-sensitivity field, the locations where an unseen object would change the action. Only this field and the support, the detections on which the current action rests, are verified at high resolution, repeatedly until the action is stable. For two planner classes, we prove that DGSP returns exactly the action of whole-frame high-resolution perception if crop detections match whole-frame ones and the crops cover the field, conditions that real images meet approximately. On three driving datasets, it reproduces this action on about 98% of frames with about a quarter of the pixels. At the pixel cost of uniform downscaling, it repairs more of the draft's disagreements with this action, brakes falsely less often, and recovers many more of the decision-relevant objects that the draft misses.

title: Data and Code for: Reliability, Refusal, and Multilingual Content Moderation across Heterogeneous LLM Providers (Benchmark v2.4-final)
abstract: This record contains the frozen benchmark package v2.4-final that underlies the article Dinler, B. (2026). Reliability, Refusal, and Multilingual Content Moderation across Heterogeneous LLM Providers: A Prompt-Matched Study of Anthropic, OpenAI, and DeepSeek. AI and Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-026-01539-9 Author: Burhan Dinler, Independent Researcher, ORCID 0009-0007-1167-2012 Study design. The benchmark has 32 canonical prompts, each in four languages: German, English, Mandarin Chinese and Northern Kurdish (Kurmanji). That gives 128 prompt variants. Each variant was sent to three providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek) in one execution window on 21 September 2026, for 384 responses in total. The responses were blinded, annotated by a primary and a secondary annotator per language, adjudicated, and analysed with prompt-clustered GEE models.

title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents
abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.

title: Fully Parallel Multi-Agent Photonic Optimizer
abstract: Abstract Optimization problems are central to many important cross-disciplinary applications. In their conventional implementations, the sequential nature of operations imposes strict limitations on the computational efficiency. Here, we discuss how analog optical computing can overcome this fundamental bottleneck. We propose a photonic optimizer unit, together with supporting algorithms that uses in-memory computation within a nature-inspired, multi-agent cooperative framework. The system performs a sequence of reconfigurable parallel matrix–vector operations, enabled by the high bandwidth and multiplexing capabilities inherent to photonic circuits. This approach provides a pathway toward fast paced and high-quality solutions for difficult optimization and search problems.

title: Il peso della pioggia. L'intelligenza artificiale dal neurone ai modelli che ragionano
abstract: Il libro è un dialogo tra un allievo e un Maestro, in un dojo di karate affacciato sul mare. Nel dojo si impara ripetendo, sbagliando e correggendo, un gesto alla volta: è così che impara una rete. In mare si naviga con strumenti precisi dentro un mondo che non lo è: il vento si legge ma non si comanda, il tempo si prevede solo per qualche giorno, e non ci si fida mai di un solo strumento: è così che si usa un modello. Soprattutto teorie consolidate: il neurone, l'allenamento, le reti che guardano e che leggono, gli embedding, i Transformer, i modelli di linguaggio e il modo in cui vengono educati e serviti. Sono le idee che non cambiano ogni sei mesi, e sono quelle che servono per capire le nuove. La promessa è questa: alla fine saprete prendere qualsiasi annuncio e chiedervi in quale lezione cade, quale problema risolve, a quale prezzo, e se è sostanza o rumore. Versione 2.0, 17 novembre 2026. Testo in italiano, 316 pagine A4.

title: Chorus: Shared N-gram Embeddings with Layer-wise Adaptation
abstract: Language models can gain capacity at little computational cost from n-gram embedding tables: large tables of learned vectors for short sequences of consecutive tokens, which are looked up and added to the model's input or to its intermediate layers. Recent designs commonly use a separate n-gram embedding table for each layer, which makes the tables costly in memory and prevents layers from sharing what they learn. Sharing a single table, however, gives every layer the same embedding and leaves no room for layer-wise preferences, and it performs poorly in practice. We propose Chorus, in which one set of n-gram embedding tables serves the whole network and every layer reads it in its own way. Each layer maps the refined embedding through its own projection layer, after rescaling its components by factors computed from its current hidden state. Chorus matches the quality of existing n-gram methods with 87% smaller tables: with 1.2B table parameters it predicts text better than FactorEngram and DeepSeek's Engram do with 9.6B. It outperforms Engram, TN-gram and FactorEngram in every setting where we compared them, across table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters. We also show that the recently proposed memory-efficient optimizer Ember works well with Chorus, saving 99.2% of table-optimizer memory compared with AdamW without degrading training performance. These results enable further scaling of n-gram embedding tables along the table-size axis by reducing memory use and allowing shared knowledge to be reused across layers.

title: When a Larger Guidance Scale Repairs Text-to-Video Failures and When It Does Not
abstract: When a text-to-video diffusion model ignores part of a prompt, the usual first fix is to raise the classifier-free guidance scale. This paper is a measurement study of when that fix works. On Mochi, the same increase repairs failures on rare compositions ("a snowy beach") beyond what generating again does, does not repair negations ("a highway with no vehicles"), where it fixes fewer failures than generating again does, and changes nothing for events that must happen late in a clip ("a sandcastle that a wave washes flat"). Which of these happens can be known in advance, from the prompt and one inexpensive score. The score, which we call demand, measures how strongly the denoiser reacts to the part of the prompt that the failed video leaves out, and it is read from the first quarter of denoising, before any video exists. Our main finding is a condition: raising the scale is effective only when the prompt contains no negation and no event tied to a specific time, and when demand is sufficiently high, with recovery clearly higher above a fitted threshold than below it. Published corrections for the three failure types, used as fixed probes, behave as this account predicts. A short decision rule follows: before generating again, a user can tell whether the most common fix is worth trying, and what to use when it is not.

title: Near-Heisenberg-limited parallel amplitude estimation with logarithmic-depth circuits
abstract: Quantum amplitude estimation is one of the core subroutines in quantum algorithms. This paper gives a parallelized amplitude estimation (PAE) algorithm that simultaneously achieves near-Heisenberg scaling in the total number of queries and sub-linear scaling in the circuit depth, with respect to the estimation precision. The algorithm is composed of a global GHZ state followed by separated low-depth Grover circuits optimized by quantum signal processing techniques; the number of qubits in the GHZ state and the depth of each circuit is tunable as a trade-off way, which particularly enables even near-Heisenberg-limited and logarithmic-depth algorithm for amplitude estimation. We prove that this trade-off scaling is nearly optimal with use of the parallel quantum adversary method, against folklore on the impossibility of efficient parallelization in amplitude estimation. The proposed algorithm has a form of distributed quantum computing, which may be suitable for device implementation.

title: A Knowledge Graph Embedding–Based Approach for Inferring Causes and Effects of Railway Operational Hazards
abstract: Railway operational hazards are interrelated and can cause accidents through cascading effects. Identifying precursor hazards and predicting subsequent hazards are necessary to prevent railway operational accidents. Knowledge graphs (KGs) explicitly encode entity relations and suit modelling such interrelated hazards. However, existing knowledge graph embedding (KGE) methods are not designed to handle combined link types induced by hazard interactivity. To address this, a novel KGE-based approach is proposed to infer both causes and effects of a target hazard from historical data. It is evaluated on a real-world railway operational hazard knowledge graph (ROHKG) built from 353 UK Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) accident reports over 2005–2023, with 948 hazard events and 1897 causal relation triples. Two novel KGE models are developed, namely a multiple semantic translation model for cause identification and a bidirectional semantic translation model for effect prediction. Both jointly integrate semantic correlation and translational distance features to mitigate mutual interference of combined link types. The models achieve Hit@10 of 84.45% and 90.24%, and mean reciprocal rank (MRR) of 0.4464 and 0.5102, for cause identification and effect prediction, respectively. They outperform leading baselines by 26.03% in MRR and 27.32% in Hit@10 for cause identification, and by 20.02% in Hit@1 for effect prediction. Both remain applicable when training data is reduced to 60% and 70% of the original corpus. These results confirm the approach’s effectiveness and robustness under data-limited conditions, providing railway operators with a basis for prioritising hazards for further assessment.

title: PeriaTrace: Tooth-Level Grounding Diagnosis and Patient-Facing Explanations from Periapical Radiographs
abstract: Periapical radiographs (PRs) are central to endodontic diagnosis, but interpreting them and preparing reports are time-consuming. Technical language can limit patients' understanding, while existing automated methods often lack tooth-level links between findings and image evidence. We present PeriaTrace, a three-stage framework integrating tooth-level diagnosis, visually grounded report generation, and patient-friendly explanations and care recommendations. PeriaTrace was developed and evaluated using 12,877 PRs from an internal dataset and two external clinical cohorts. In internal evaluation, it achieved a macro Dice coefficient of 85.35%, BLEU-4 of 0.6504, an F1 score of 94.37% for joint tooth localization and Fédération Dentaire Internationale (FDI) identification, and a grounding-tag F1 score of 77.93%. In the two external cohorts, senior endodontists considered 91.16% and 84.52% of reports suitable for retention or revision without complete rewriting. Generation averaged 4.41 seconds per PR, several tens of times faster than manual drafting. Among 196 survey participants without medical backgrounds, 96.4% preferred reports with plain-language explanations and care recommendations, and 84.7% found visual localization cues helpful. PeriaTrace may enable faster, evidence-traceable reporting while supporting clinical review and patient communication. (Abridged version)

evidence.title: PeriaTrace: Tooth-Level Grounding Diagnosis and Patient-Facing Explanations from Periapical Radiographs
evidence.abstract: Periapical radiographs (PRs) are central to endodontic diagnosis, but interpreting them and preparing reports are time-consuming. Technical language can limit patients' understanding, while existing automated methods often lack tooth-level links between findings and image evidence. We present PeriaTrace, a three-stage framework integrating tooth-level diagnosis, visually grounded report generation, and patient-friendly explanations and care recommendations. PeriaTrace was developed and evaluated using 12,877 PRs from an internal dataset and two external clinical cohorts. In internal evaluation, it achieved a macro Dice coefficient of 85.35%, BLEU-4 of 0.6504, an F1 score of 94.37% for joint tooth localization and Fédération Dentaire Internationale (FDI) identification, and a grounding-tag F1 score of 77.93%. In the two external cohorts, senior endodontists considered 91.16% and 84.52% of reports suitable for retention or revision without complete rewriting. Generation averaged 4.41 seconds per PR, several tens of times faster than manual drafting. Among 196 survey participants without medical backgrounds, 96.4% preferred reports with plain-language explanations and care recommendations, and 84.7% found visual localization cues helpful. PeriaTrace may enable faster, evidence-traceable reporting while supporting clinical review and patient communication. (Abridged version)

title: Paint: Accurate, efficient, and sparse Model Inversion via peripheral sparsification and anchor alignment
abstract: How can we reconstruct training data from a pre-trained model without access to the original dataset? Model Inversion (MI) attempts to synthesize samples similar to the training dataset. This capability is particularly useful in data-free applications, such as data-free quantization and data-free knowledge transfer, where synthetic data replace inaccessible training samples. For these applications, MI needs to generate high-fidelity samples to preserve semantic information while remaining computationally efficient, enabling scalable generation for reliable downstream performance. However, existing MI methods fail to achieve both high fidelity and efficiency simultaneously. In this paper, we propose Paint ( P eripheral sparsification and A nchor-aligned IN version T echnique), an accurate, efficient, and sparse MI framework for generating high-fidelity synthetic data. Paint integrates low-pass filtering during inversion to suppress high-frequency noise, aligns salient regions toward anchor with peripheral sparsification to preserve object structures during sparse inversion, and exploits soft targets to better capture the predictive uncertainty. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Paint improves inversion efficiency for ViTs and achieves accuracy gains of up to 5.33%p in data-free scenarios.

title: PhysScope: Agentic Multimodal Physics Reasoning with Grounded Visual Memory
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can correctly interpret physics diagrams yet apply constraints outside the states or conditions in which they hold, causing premise errors to propagate through subsequent calculations. We introduce PhysScope, an inference-time visual harness that supports self-correction of these scope mismatches without updating model weights. PhysScope enables the model to link physical scopes directly to its visual observations and explicitly constructs derived views to support reasoning. The harness imposes explicit constraints on state distinctions, conditions, and physical scopes during model reasoning, and checks agent-proposed revisions against sources and scopes. Accepted revisions invalidate registered dependents, thereby maintaining scope-aware working memory. On PhysAlign, PhysScope achieves higher solving scores than direct solving across all six evaluated VLMs. With Gemini-3.8-flash, it outperforms Canvas-CoT by 9.34 percentage points and substantially improves solving accuracy on the out-of-distribution (OOD) PhysUniBench benchmark. Ablation studies support explicit scope management and dependency maintenance as design principles for multimodal physics reasoning agents.

title: Investigating AI Incidents — Evidence, Event Reconstruction, and Causal Analysis
abstract: This report examines how investigators can establish what happened in an incident involving an AI system and identify the factors that contributed to it. It covers how to collect and verify evidence, reconstruct the sequence of events, and test competing explanations against the available record. The report considers how model behavior, deployment conditions, organizational practices, and human decisions can interact over the course of an incident. It also discusses how to document gaps in the record and explain the degree of confidence in causal findings, so that investigation results can guide corrective action and help prevent similar incidents. This publication is Report No. 19 in the Observatoire ARGA analytical report series. It includes an accompanying review.

title: Tracking Ethological Behaviors of Broiler Chickens Through Computer Vision (YoloV11) Using an Android Mobile Device
abstract: This study developed and evaluated a computer vision model for automated ethological behavior classification of broiler chickens in climate-controlled poultry houses. Using publicly available videos preprocessed and manually annotated into three classes (sitting, standing, and feeding), the YOLOv11 model was trained and deployed on an Android application via TFLite conversion. Exploratory analysis ensured dataset consistency and visual quality, while evaluation showed class-dependent performance: higher robustness for static postures (sitting, AP=0.531; precision=100%) and lower accuracy for dynamic behaviors (feeding, AP=0.292; recall=0.20). Tests with unseen images demonstrated significant improvements, achieving accuracies of 98.04% for sitting, 83.33% for standing, and 67.65% for feeding. The model showed effective generalization in real farm environments, supporting its potential for continuous behavioral monitoring, early welfare assessments, and decision-making in precision poultry farming. These findings establish a technical foundation for future mobile-based applications at commercial scale, reinforcing the role of computer vision in automated animal welfare evaluation.

title: TARE: Block Encoding Linear Combinations of Pauli Strings Without Coefficient-Dependent Ancilla State Preparation
abstract: Quantum algorithms based on Quantum Signal Processing (QSP) offer the potential for speedups across a broad range of applications, but their practical performance is often limited by the cost of constructing block encodings. We introduce Tag-and-Restore Encoding (TARE), a block-encoding method for linear combinations of Pauli strings. Unlike Linear Combination of Unitaries (LCU), which prepares a coefficient-dependent ancilla state, TARE moves the coefficient loading to the system register. Coefficient magnitudes are absorbed into a unitary built from mutually anticommuting Pauli strings acting on the system register. These Pauli strings are then mapped to the target Pauli strings through appropriate transformations, yielding a block encoding of the target operator. The ancilla register size scales logarithmically with the number of Pauli strings and can be extended to larger registers to provide a width-depth trade-off. We benchmark TARE against four LCU constructions for the transverse-field Ising model, the Jordan-Wigner representation of a fermionic star Hamiltonian, and random Pauli-string operators. Our numerical results suggest a potential advantage for fermionic Hamiltonians with long-range hopping, especially when two-qubit gates and ancilla qubits are scarce.

title: Contained or Escaped? Measuring Sandbox Escape and Auto-Reviewer Decisions in AI Coding Agents
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) coding agents now run shell commands in a default sandbox and must request permission, often screened by a large language model (LLM) auto-reviewer, before a command may use the network or write outside the workspace. Most prompt-injection benchmarks for coding agents assume unrestricted execution. We built SARD-Bench, 240 poisoned-workspace cases in four families and three stealth tiers, with a harness whose single tool makes the agent declare and justify the permissions it needs. We ran Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-5.1 and Llama 4 Maverick once per case (720 trajectories), executed the two-turn family in a macOS Seatbelt sandbox, and had a GPT-4o-mini reviewer judge every harmful command with and without the agent’s rationale. All labels were audited by hand in two passes. The two proprietary models ran the payload inside the sandbox in 28.3% of runs and requested the privileges to escape in 6.5%. Llama 4 Maverick escaped in 44.6%. Stealthier files raised in-sandbox execution from 10.6% to 50.6% but left escape rates unchanged. With the agent’s rationale, the reviewer blocked 126 of 138 escape requests, against 64 from the command alone. Claude Sonnet 5.5 returned provider refusals in 140 runs, and an indicator-matching scorer missed half of all escapes. Evaluations of sandboxed agents should report where a payload would run and audit their labels by hand.

title: Residual-Guided Lightweight Reinforcement Learning for Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection with a Frozen World Model
abstract: In automated driving, world models provide future scene predictions for evaluating candidate trajectories, but fixed selection rules may not capture scene-dependent trade-offs. We propose a residual-guided reinforcement learning (RL) framework for lightweight trajectory selection with a frozen world model and a fixed candidate bank. The framework uses proximal policy optimization (PPO) to fine-tune a joint policy over candidate selection and bounded trajectory residuals. A context-conditioned ranking network learns candidate preferences from feedback obtained by evaluating local perturbations of the selected trajectories. At inference, the selector combines learned preference and predicted risk ranks using fixed weights and returns the selected candidate trajectory without modification. Fine-tuning updates 16,106 parameters across the actor and critic, while the deployed selector retains only the 11,725-parameter ranking network, with the residual branch and critic used exclusively during training. In open-loop evaluation on the nuScenes validation set, the method reduces average Euclidean trajectory error (L2) by 3.99% relative to the RiskWorld model baseline without RL-based selection. Under matched budgets for feedback accesses and actor updates, residual exploration reduces L2 by 0.83% relative to the categorical PPO variant trained without residuals. The method also maintains lower L2 than RiskWorld when risk features are removed or shuffled.

title: Direct vs. Indirect Goal Signals in Multi-Agent RL Tasks
abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning tasks require agents to cooperate with teammates to achieve a shared objective. One important challenge in such settings is resolving uncertainty about a teammate’s goal. Goal information can be provided directly through an explicit goal signal or inferred indirectly from the teammate’s behaviour. In this thesis, we investigate the relative usefulness of direct and indirect goal signals in a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning task. We then identify the environmental properties under which each type of signal is more advantageous. We consider a two-agent gridworld environment consisting of a leader that knows the task goal and a follower that must cooperate with the leader to complete the task. Based on how the follower uses each type of information, we introduce two policy-based heuristics, one for each type of goal signal, to estimate the additional number of steps required when that signal is unavailable. These heuristics help us develop intuition about which type of goal signal allows the agents to complete the task more efficiently in a specific map. We then design five additional experiments that modify different properties of the environment and progressively increase the difficulty of the task to examine how the heuristic predictions change. Finally, we compare these predictions with the performance of follower policies trained using PPO. The results show that neither direct nor indirect goal information is universally more useful. Direct goal information is more beneficial when the primary source of uncertainty is the teammate’s goal, whereas indirect information can be more useful when uncertainty concerns the teammate’s plan. In several settings, the PPO experiments generally agree with the heuristics in their rankings of the goal signals. However, they also reveal cases in which the theoretically preferred behaviour is difficult to learn because of partial observability or exploration challenges. Overall, the heuristics provide a theoretical basis for understanding how different environmental properties affect the usefulness of each goal signal, while the PPO results demonstrate that learned policies may not always discover the effective behaviours assumed by the heuristics.

title: The Rhythm of Generated Video: Latent Chunking Leaves Periodic Traces in Compressed Bitstreams
abstract: Most AI-generated video detectors analyze decoded pixels and overlook how videos are produced. We show that causal video autoencoders leave an architecture-specific rhythm in compressed bitstreams: their temporal stride concentrates unpredictable content at latent-chunk boundaries, so rate-distortion optimized encoders allocate bits periodically. Without decoding pixels, we observe four-frame pulses in CogVideoX and Wan2.2 and eight-frame pulses in LTX-Video, which are absent from content-matched camera footage. Passing camera footage through a generator's autoencoder alone induces the pulse, supporting its proposed origin. A training-free peak-ratio statistic separates generated from camera video (AUC 0.84-0.94) and persists across tested quantization settings and H.264/H.265 encoding. Frame-size traces also identify four commercial generators, with 89.2%, 84.1%, and 83.0% accuracy under H.264, H.265, and AV1, beating the pixel-based UnivFD baseline (72.7-73.6%). Our results directly link generative architecture to measurable coding demand.

title: Quantum feedback algorithms for DNA assembly using FALQON variants
abstract: Abstract Reconstructing DNA sequences without a reference, known as de novo assembly, is a complex computational task involving the alignment of overlapping fragments. To address this problem, a usual strategy is to map the assembly to a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) formulation, which can be solved by different quantum algorithms. In this work, we focus on standard Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON) and two previously proposed feedback-based variants, which update control parameters without an external classical parameter-optimization routine. We analyze DNA sequence fragments from SARS-CoV-2 and human mitochondrial DNA using standard FALQON, second-order FALQON (SO-FALQON), and time-rescaled FALQON (TR-FALQON). Numerical results show that both variants can improve convergence and success probability while requiring fewer feedback layers than standard FALQON in selected configurations. These results support the use of enhanced feedback dynamics as a proof-of-concept strategy for reduced DNA-assembly instances, while practical scalability and hardware performance remain open questions.

title: A Brief Tutorial on Reinforcement Learning: From MDP to DDPG
abstract: Following the evolution from theoretical foundations to advanced deep learning algorithms, a coherent overview of reinforcement learning (RL) is proposed in this tutorial. We begin with the mathematical formalization of sequential decision-making via Markov decision processes (MDPs). In MDPs, the Bellman equation and the Bellman optimality equation play important roles; they provide the basis for policy evaluation and the fundamental condition for optimal behavior, respectively. The movement from these equations to practical algorithms is explored, starting with model-based dynamic programming and progressing to model-free temporal-difference (TD) learning. As a pivotal model-free algorithm, Q-learning directly implements the Bellman optimality equation through sampling. To handle high-dimensional state spaces, function approximation and deep reinforcement learning emerge, exemplified by deep Q-networks (DQN). Thereafter, actor-critic methods address the challenge of continuous action spaces. As a typical actor-critic scheme, the deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) algorithm is illustrated in detail to show how it adapts the principles of optimality to continuous control by maintaining separate actor and critic networks. Finally, the tutorial concludes with a unified perspective, observing the development of RL as a logical progression from defining optimality conditions to developing scalable solution algorithms. Furthermore, future directions are summarized.

title: CAST: Calibrating Correspondences for Training-Free Biomedical In-Context Segmentation
abstract: Biomedical image segmentation must keep up with new anatomical structures, subjects, imaging modalities, and acquisition protocols, yet dense expert annotations are scarce and models trained on one cohort often struggle to transfer. In-context segmentation (ICS) offers a way out: a new structure is specified by a few annotated exemplars at inference time. However, reliable correspondence remains challenging in biomedical images, where adjacent structures often share similar appearances, and variations across subjects and imaging conditions further obscure their distinctions. We introduce CAST, a training-free framework built on a frozen DINOv3 backbone to calibrate fine-grained correspondences. Its stability test improves feature reliability at both global and patch-specific levels, while its coherence test assesses whether candidate correspondences are supported by consistent local structural context. Together, these tests enable more reliable correspondence across diverse anatomical structures and imaging conditions. Across eight biomedical benchmarks spanning 2D and 3D segmentation, cross-subject, and cross-modality transfer, CAST outperforms the strongest overall baseline by 12.34 percentage points in Dice and ranks first across all six volumetric settings. The versatility of CAST further opens up opportunities for challenging biomedical applications, including 2D-to-3D segmentation and atlas label transfer.

title: Unsupervised cross-domain adaptation for wearable-based human activity recognition
abstract: Abstract Recent advancements in deep learning-based wearable human action recognition (wHAR) have improved the capture and classification of complex motions. Still, adoption remains limited due to the lack of expert annotations and domain discrepancies from user variations. Limited annotations hinder the model’s ability to generalize to out-of-distribution samples. While data augmentation can improve generalizability, unsupervised augmentation techniques must be applied carefully to avoid introducing noise. Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) addresses domain discrepancies by aligning conditional distributions with labeled target samples, but vanilla pseudo-labeling can lead to error propagation. To address these challenges, we propose CoHAR , a novel joint optimization architecture comprised of three functions: (i) consistency regularizer between augmented samples to improve model classification generalizability, (ii) temporal ensemble for robust pseudo-label generation, and (iii) conditional distribution alignment to improve domain generalizability. The temporal ensemble works by aggregating predictions from past epochs to smooth out noisy pseudo-label predictions, which are then used in the conditional distribution alignment module to minimize kernel-based class-wise conditional maximum mean discrepancy ( k CMMD) between the source and target feature space to learn a domain-invariant embedding. The consistency-regularized augmentations ensure that multiple augmentations of the same sample share the same labels; this results in (a) strong generalization with limited source domain samples and (b) consistent pseudo-label generation in target samples. The novel integration of these three modules in CoHAR results in a range of $$\varvec{\approx } {\varvec{4}}--{\varvec{12\%}}$$ ≈ 4 - - 12 % average macro-F1 score improvement over six state-of-the-art UDA methods in five benchmark wHAR datasets.

To address these challenges, we propose CoHAR , a novel joint optimization architecture comprised of three functions: (i) consistency regularizer between augmented samples to improve model classification generalizability, (ii) temporal ensemble for robust pseudo-label generation, and (iii) conditional distribution alignment to improve domain generalizability. The temporal ensemble works by aggregating predictions from past epochs to smooth out noisy pseudo-label predictions, which are then used in the conditional distribution alignment module to minimize kernel-based class-wise conditional maximum mean discrepancy ( k CMMD) between the source and target feature space to learn a domain-invariant embedding. The consistency-regularized augmentations ensure that multiple augmentations of the same sample share the same labels; this results in (a) strong generalization with limited source domain samples and (b) consistent pseudo-label generation in target samples. The novel integration of these three modules in CoHAR results in a range of $$\varvec{\approx } {\varvec{4}}--{\varvec{12\%}}$$ ≈ 4 - - 12 % average macro-F1 score improvement over six state-of-the-art UDA methods in five benchmark wHAR datasets.

title: RagHarnessDebugger: Jev-Guided Agentic RAG in Contract Inference Repair Auditing
abstract: Agentic systems using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must repair their own answers by gathering more evidence, testing alternative policies and deciding if, when, and what repairs are needed. Yet how do we know if a system's repairs are working when metrics like accuracy can be misleading? We present RagHarnessDebugger, a framework that records every repair decision in a Jev-guided harness for contract inference and audits the record to facilitate complete debugging of all decisions taken during a RAG repair journey. RagHarnessDebugger checks that each trace is intact, that each validation applies to the candidate it is counted for, and which answers the acceptance rule can reach. We tested our approach on ContractNLI non-disclosure agreements with two reader models and a replication set of separate contracts. Our debugger's audit layer exposed failure patterns that were hidden under aggregate metrics, policies acceptance cost of repairs vs regressions and policy acceptance gap of 77% and 76% of available but unrealised repairs on development and replication sets. Our audit, together with a labeled error analysis and replay mechanism, allowed following the execution path all the way to the terminal decision - uncovering where missing repairs became lost. Our revised harness improved accuracy over the initial BM25-only baseline by 3.6 points on development contracts and 3.7 points on the replication set, and even improved our full contract access reference score by 1.1 on development and 2.4 on replication set. While our work here demonstrates how the debugger can conduct decision root-cause analysis for missed repairs, the true value lies with providing this debugger for judgment visibility serving continuous improvement of RAG decisions and their explainability. Keywords: agentic RAG, AI evidence repair, harness explainability, counterfactual replay, Jev, ContractNLI

title: Arctic Puffin Algorithm with local escaping operator for feature selection in high-dimensional datasets
abstract: Abstract Large datasets might make data mining more difficult due to their high dimensionality. To minimize the dimensionality of large datasets, feature selection is an essential step that maximizes classification accuracy by choosing the most informative features. In this study, a binary adaptation of the enhanced Arctic Puffin Optimization (EAPO) algorithm, which builds on the Arctic Puffin Optimization (APO) algorithm, is introduced within a wrapper-based framework to identify the optimal subset of features for classification tasks. To improve the search performance of APO, a local escaping operator is incorporated to effectively balance exploration and exploitation and enhance its ability to escape local optima. Furthermore, a key aspect of EAPO is the design of the transfer function, which facilitates the transformation of the continuous search space into a binary domain. To evaluate its effectiveness, three transfer functions, S-shaped, V-shaped, and U-shaped, are investigated. The proposed EAPO method is assessed on 14 benchmark datasets using the k-Nearest Neighbor classifier as the evaluation metric. To control overfitting, k-fold cross-validation employs a partitioning strategy in which the dataset is divided into k folds, and each fold is used as the test set once while the remaining folds form the training set. Comparisons are made with state-of-the-art methods, including the beluga whale optimization, sine cosine algorithm, kepler optimization algorithm, grey wolf optimizer, coati optimization algorithm, salp swarm algorithm, arithmetic optimization algorithm, and bat optimization algorithm. The results obtained from the experiments show that the EAPO technique is better in terms of consistency, feature reduction, and classification accuracy. Statistical analysis further confirms the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method.

title: How Web Research Agents Interpret User Priorities
abstract: Web research agents gather information online and write cited reports, including financial analysis. Users can state a priority to guide this research, but a priority may not say how to judge the options, leaving the agent to choose the criteria. We examine how two such agents, built on OpenAI and Anthropic models, interpret a stated priority. In 36 runs, the agents compared Microsoft and Alphabet as businesses. Prompts asked for special attention to growth or resilience, or gave no priority. We analyzed reports, searches, returned sources and cited sources. Of the 24 reports given a priority, 21 focused on it, but their criteria varied. Under the growth priority, OpenAI reports that ranked the companies accounted for risk or predictability and favored Microsoft, while the Anthropic ones judged growth by its pace and favored Alphabet. Under the resilience priority, reports used partly different criteria, and most named Microsoft as the more resilient company. Of the search and source measures tested, only the Anthropic agent's search wording differed detectably by condition. These findings suggest evaluations should examine the criteria behind a report's judgements, not only its focus or accuracy. Interfaces could let users see and adjust those criteria.

title: Structured AI ideation yields physical strategies for epithelial barrier repair
abstract: AI systems increasingly support literature analysis, candidate evaluation and hypothesis refinement, but enabling researchers to explore research directions beyond established disciplinary approaches remains challenging. We developed Abelio, an AI system designed to generate novel research directions by expanding investigators' avenues of inquiry. Abelio reformulates research objectives, uses these alternative formulations to identify relevant elements outside conventional disciplinary boundaries, and refines the resulting hypotheses. Each stage integrates divergent exploration with convergent selection through a dedicated subsystem. In quantitative evaluations, proposals generated by the Ideation Core (Abelio's hypothesis-generation core) outperformed those of four frontier large language models in scientific soundness and hypothesis diversity, and three of four in distance from existing literature. Subsystem ablation showed that each subsystem contributes to the property it targets, with the contribution of Element Selection measurable before Refinement. To investigate intestinal epithelial barrier restoration, Abelio proposed physical interventions involving membrane-tethered poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and cholesterol-anchored complementary DNA. Both proposals were archived before experimentation and subsequently tested independently in damaged Caco-2 monolayers. PEG preserved barrier function in a membrane-surface-dependent manner, whereas complementary DNA enabled sequence-specific restoration that was reversible on demand. These findings demonstrate how structured research ideation can identify experimentally testable approaches beyond established disciplinary conventions.

title: Copyright and the Training of Generative AI Models
abstract: This report examines how copyright applies to the use of protected works in generative AI training. It considers where legal questions arise across the training data lifecycle, from collecting and copying material to documenting its use in a model. The report covers licensing, text and data mining exceptions, rights reservations, and transparency requirements for providers of general-purpose AI models. It also explores what records developers can maintain to substantiate their decisions and what evidence independent auditors can use to assess those practices. This publication is Report No. 23 in the Observatoire ARGA analytical report series.

title: PAIR: Bringing Household Robots into the Smart Home
abstract: Household robots often need to operate appliances, and smart appliances offer both control panels and device APIs. Existing embodied AI simulation environments, however, model appliances solely as physical objects. We introduce PAIR, a smart-home simulation environment grounded in the Matter protocol~https://csa-iot.org/all-solutions/matter/, the industry standard for smart-home devices. PAIR provides 84 smart-device assets whose functional control panels and APIs act on a shared device state, with ambient conditions that evolve in response to both. From a survey of 1,443 requests, we construct a benchmark of 40 tasks that all require object manipulation yet remain solvable without API access, with 340 human demonstrations for policy training. Whether run alone, with a high-level planner, or with an API-enabled planner, two fine-tuned VLA policies complete none of the 120 evaluation episodes. Robots rarely get far enough to use the API: even with oracle plans and API access, over 90\% of failed rollouts stall at navigating, grasping, or operating a door. With a perfect oracle in place of the robot's body, the best planner still gets through only 57.3\% of its plan. When choosing between pressing a button and calling an API, several planners go by whether they can read the panel, not by API latency.We will release our code and data upon publication.

title: SpikWM: Efficient End-to-End Spiking World Modeling for Visual Planning
abstract: Goal-conditioned planning with image observations and goals requires predictions that distinguish visual states and action consequences. Spiking neural networks offer sparse computation, but single-step spikes can obscure motion cues and merge actions with different physical outcomes. We propose the Spiking Latent World Model (SpikWM), an end-to-end joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) with one simulation step per image and one neural update per latent position. Spiking Regional Encoding retains spatial cues through regional pooling. Bi-Spike Action Encoding combines positive and negative binary responses, while Causal Membrane Prediction carries subthreshold evidence across the latent history with learned group-wise time constants. The encoder and predictor are trained jointly on reward-free image--action trajectories using next-embedding prediction and SIGReg. With a common planner, SpikWM achieves mean success rates of $88.67\%$, $97.33\%$, $99.33\%$, and $86.67\%$ on Push-T, Two-Room, Reacher, and OGBench-Cube, respectively, outperforming two spiking baselines. Push-T ablations support each module, and controlled replays examine responses to appearance and physical state changes. Under a matched planning budget, SpikWM reduces estimated arithmetic energy by $75.6\%$ relative to LeWM. Code will be released at https://github.com/ShawnYE618/SpikWM.

title: Large Language Models Have Not Yet Transformed Science
abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) in late 2022 has raised questions about the future of science, but assessing their impact requires understanding how scientific practices were already evolving. We analyze 2.5 million full-text papers across five disciplines from 2015 to 2025, tracing trends over a broad spectrum of lexical, structural, epistemological, and social dimensions. Aside from frequency shifts in some words, most pre-2023 trends continued with limited detectable breaks. Among the notable exceptions, growth in computer science coauthor teams accelerated significantly in Asia, while apparent declines in biomedical topic diversity largely reflected standardization in article formats. Our study establishes an empirical foundation for monitoring the health of global science as LLM adoption deepens.

title: Quantum noise suppression at scale with crosstalk-robust gate sets
abstract: We introduce crosstalk-robust gate sets, which are obtained using a novel, scalable optimal control problem exploiting quantum crosstalk’s pairwise operator structure. Crosstalk-robust gate sets suppress quantum crosstalk throughout arbitrary computations, whereas conventional dynamical decoupling primarily targets idle periods. We use the IBM Quantum Platform as a testbed for our gate sets, where we study their efficacy via error suppression protocols and randomized parallel single-qubit circuits of up to eight qubits. Using a Hamiltonian simulation of a four-qubit transverse field Ising model, we show that crosstalk-robust gate sets enhance median algorithmic performance by a factor of four over baseline Gaussian gates using the same calibration procedures. Lastly, we provide numerical evidence that crosstalk-robust gate sets can enable larger qubit-qubit coupling strengths that can cut two-qubit gate times in half, demonstrating how hardware-software co-design using quantum optimal control can create new opportunities for quantum computing architectures.

title: Faster Classical and Quantum BKW for LWE
abstract: We improve classical and quantum BKW for learning with errors at Regev's parameters. Each coded round sets a separate radius limit for each earlier coordinate block. A tighter limit in a later round allows wider rounding bins when the block first enters, but makes suitable pairs harder to find. Choosing these limits together with the block sizes gives classical time $2^{0.8883n+o(n)}$ and quantum time $2^{0.8737n+o(n)}$ with Grover search. Reusing a quantum-walk state to find many pairs lowers the time to $2^{0.8643n+o(n)}$. These algorithms read fresh classical samples. From only $\Theta(n\log n)$ original samples, amplification gives classical time $2^{1.6359n+o(n)}$, quantum time $2^{1.6130n+o(n)}$ with Grover search, and $2^{1.5979n+o(n)}$ with reusable walks. Integral equations define the constants in these bounds. The running times are heuristic: we assume that the intermediate lists have the distance and filter statistics of independent random directions within each block. The walk also needs these statistics inside its filters and coherent reads and writes of working memory.

title: DiCEGI Diversified Counterfactual Explanations for a Group of Instances
abstract: Machine learning techniques are now essential in many critical real-world domains to support decision-making. However, expert users often need explanations for the decisions made by these models. One key approach to explainable AI is using counterfactual explanations. These involve making small changes to input instances and observing how the machine learning model’s decision changes. For explaining outcomes for a group of instances, the explainer should identify a few diverse small interventions that are relevant to most of those instances rather than providing explanations for each one individually. In a classification setting that may involve multiple labels, we introduce a method called $$\text {DiCE}_{GI}$$ that relies on an augmented Lagrangian method to identify the optimal set of perturbations to apply collectively to a group of instances. Experiments conducted on both artificial and real datasets demonstrate that $$\text {DiCE}_{GI}$$ consistently returns the set of K interventions minimizing cost and maximizing coverage and diversity.

title: VITAL: A Framework for Validating Agentic AI in Pharmaceutical Drug Development and Clinical Trial Operations
abstract: Current assurance approaches do not establish whether evidence is sufficient to validate, monitor and govern agentic artificial intelligence (AI) within a pharmaceutical context of use. Plausible outputs may conceal failures in retrieval, reasoning, orchestration or human-control points, where reference standards are unavailable. We developed and operationalised VITAL (Validation by Intended use, Traceability, Autonomy and Lifecycle evidence), a validation framework for agents in clinical development, through landscape analysis, regulatory and standards mapping, expert interviews and multi-stakeholder refinement. VITAL integrates context of use, controls, behavioural validation and lifecycle evidence within a risk-adjusted framework. We applied VITAL across epidemiology and treatment-landscape analysis, site selection, enrolment rescue and trial-design trade-off support to translate autonomy, reversibility, transparency and patient impact into proportionate validation activities, evidence requirements and auditable reconstruction of system behaviour. VITAL may inform evidence requirements and lifecycle accountability for higher-risk pharmaceutical uses; evaluation should assess reproducibility across assessors, organisations and system configurations.

title: Provenance and uncertainty in sensor fusion for defensive military intelligence
abstract: Abstract Objective: How can correlation between sensors be prevented from being mistaken for independent corroboration? Method: purposive documentary synthesis and dependency analysis from a military intelligence perspective, comparing public technical and institutional references. Evidence, inference and exercise assumptions are distinguished. Results: the study proposes a justification chain, defensive architecture and response flowchart, together with observables for future evaluation. Fusion should preserve lineage, quality and alternative interpretations through to the authorised decision. The contribution links observed capability, competent authority and risk acceptance. No experimental measurements were obtained and operational effectiveness was not estimated. Interoperability references and NIST frameworks are applied within their scope and do not constitute certification. Conclusion: Confidence in an estimate depends on tracing its observations and dependencies. A defensible sensor architecture preserves uncertainty and supports correction of products already shared. The model requires external review and authorised testing before adoption.

title: EvoCoT: Co-evolving generation and verification for LLM-based optimization autoformulation
abstract: Formulating optimization models from natural-language specifications is a major bottleneck in engineering decision-making, because accurate translation requires both domain expertise and strict modeling discipline. Existing large language model (LLM) approaches show strong code-generation ability but often produce formulations that are executable yet semantically incorrect, or structurally invalid under solver constraints. Evolutionary Chain-of-Thought Optimization (EvoCoT) is introduced as a co-evolutionary autoformulation framework that treats model synthesis as guided discrete search over reasoning--code pairs rather than one-shot generation. EvoCoT combines three tightly coupled mechanisms: chain-of-thought evolutionary refinement for semantic exploration, memory-guided exemplar retrieval for reusing successful modeling patterns, and a co-evolving verifier that continuously acquires formulation knowledge during search and delivers dense structural-faithfulness feedback unavailable to static verifiers. Verifier feedback and retrieved successes directly regulate selection and regeneration, forming a feedback-regulated closed loop that progressively improves formulation faithfulness and solver robustness. Experiments on eight benchmark suites, including NL4OPT, MAMO, BWOR, IndustryOR, OptMATH, and ComplexOR, show consistent gains over strong zero-shot, agentic, and fine-tuned baselines, with the largest improvements on difficult industrial-scale tasks. The results demonstrate that co-evolving generation and verification is a practical pathway toward reliable, scalable, and solver-executable optimization autoformulation.

title: ADIRO: AEC Drawing Information Representation Ontologies
abstract: ADIRO (AEC Drawing Information Representation Ontologies) is a suite of OWL/TTL ontologies for representing drawings of the architecture, engineering and construction (AEC) domain: drawing metadata, common symbols, domain-common and domain-specific symbols, the geometry of what is found on a drawing, and the provenance and confidence of what is extracted from it. It supports machine-learning tasks, in particular information extraction, and lets drawings drive graph databases and knowledge graphs. Each module of the suite has its own IRI, version and documentation page.

title: Rescaling OLS-Merged Adapters To Improve Personalized Image Generation
abstract: Merging multiple adapters into a single image generation model reduces deployment costs while preserving diverse task capabilities or personalization modes. State-of-the-art methods such as RegMean, Mix-of-Show, and Subspace Routing fit the outputs of the merged model to those of the individual adapters using ordinary least squares (OLS). We show that this reconstruction objective systematically shrinks task-specific signals whenever the activation distributions of different tasks overlap, producing a merged adapter that is too weak for downstream use. We derive a decomposition that quantifies this shrinkage and propose rescaling the merged update to restore signal strength. On multi-subject personalization with up to 30 merged adapters, rescaling substantially improves subject fidelity over unscaled baselines. Our approach also improves results on style transfer, concept erasure, image classification, and LLM-based text classification.

title: Explainability Metrics for Object Detection Models
abstract: Object detection models based on deep learning achieve state-of-the-art accuracy in many applications, but their predictions are difficult to interpret. Existing explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques for computer vision mostly focus on image classification, and their direct extension to object detection is non-trivial, as detectors must explain both what was detected (class) and where it was detected (bounding box). In this paper, we revisit perturbation-based saliency methods for object detection, with a particular focus on D-RISE, a popular model-agnostic technique. We highlight practical limitations of D-RISE, particularly the absence of a detector-specific importance score aligned with detection performance. We then propose a novel detection-loss based explainability score that quantifies the importance of each image region through the deterioration of the detector’s loss under random masking. The proposed score jointly accounts for classification confidence and localisation quality, and it is normalised to be in [0, 1], providing an interpretable per-pixel importance measure. The proposed score is evaluated on three datasets covering industrial and general-object detection scenarios. In addition to qualitative visualization, we report object-level explainability statistics and deletion-based fidelity analysis to assess the alignment between highlighted regions and detection confidence. The results indicate that the proposed $$\varDelta $$ -based scoring method produces consistent and interpretable saliency maps that are directly linked to changes in detection loss. Overall, the proposed approach establishes a principled link between visual explanations and detection performance, and paves the way for robust, quantitative comparison of XAI methods for object detection.

title: MI-Hyper: Generating Multiple Instance Models for Weight Space Transfer Learning in Histopathology via Mixed Tasks Pretrained HyperNetwork
abstract: Zero-shot whole-slide image (WSI) prediction aims to generalize to new pathology tasks without parameter updates at deployment. MI-Zero makes these predictions by pooling patch-text similarities. Conditional weight generation, combined with supervision from diverse pathology tasks, offers an alternative: learning to construct predictive rules from task descriptions. We introduce MI-Hyper, a hypernetwork pretrained across mixed tasks to generate the aggregation and classification weights of multiple instance learning (MIL) models. We first train the generator and a shared MIL basis jointly using source labels. We then freeze the basis and refine the generator. The generated task weights are reused across cases. Across 308 tasks from 52 pathology datasets, MI-Hyper improves mean AUC, balanced accuracy and macro-F1 over MI-Zero by 1.85, 1.17 and 0.57 percentage points, respectively. On some molecular prediction tasks, both AUC and balanced accuracy improve by more than 20 points. These results support task-conditioned weight generation as a promising approach to weight-space transfer for long-sequence modeling.

title: Generative AI Conversation Acceptance: The First Unified Framework for Bidirectional and Unidirectional Acceptance of Conversational Invitations Across Human and Artificial Intelligence Agents
abstract: The development of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has substantially expanded the possibilities of conversational interaction, enabling humans and AI agents to initiate, participate in, coordinate, and sustain increasingly complex communication processes. However, the mechanisms through which an invited participant explicitly accepts an invitation to establish a conversation have not been sufficiently conceptualized as an independent and unified interaction capability. Existing research has investigated proactive dialogue initiation, mixed-initiative interaction, conversational topic suggestions, dialogue management, and technology acceptance. Nevertheless, these research areas generally examine different aspects of conversational participation rather than establishing a comprehensive framework specifically dedicated to the acceptance of conversational invitations across heterogeneous participants. To address this conceptual gap, this paper proposes Generative AI Conversation Acceptance (GACA), a unified framework for accepting conversational invitations among human users and generative AI agents. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to explicitly formulate conversation acceptance as an independent, cross-participant interaction capability and integrate bidirectional and unidirectional acceptance into a unified conceptual architecture. The framework encompasses human-to-human, human-to-AI, AI-to-human, and AI-to-AI interactions. It further introduces a structured set of acceptance mechanisms, including explicit, conditional, scheduled, delayed, partial, automatic, reciprocal, selective, context-aware, and revocable acceptance. The proposed framework distinguishes invitation issuance, invitation reception, acceptance decision-making, acceptance confirmation, and conversation establishment as separate operational stages. It also incorporates participant authorization, invitation expiration, privacy protection, refusal handling, and acceptance-state management. This paper establishes the conceptual foundations, architectural components, operational principles, research propositions, and evaluation dimensions necessary for implementing conversation acceptance in future generative AI communication systems. The contribution is intended to extend conversational AI research beyond the generation and initiation of dialogue toward the systematic management of whether, when, and under what conditions an invited participant agrees to communicate.
